speakeroldname: Hon. George Prudham (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):

subtopic: SURVEY OF IRON ORE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the last sitting of the house the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Laing) asked me to make a statement with regard to the proposals of the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys to survey iron ore in the province of British Columbia.
The geological survey of Canada has already made considerable investigation of the British Columbia iron ore deposits. Investigations made prior to 1925 were compiled in a report by G. A. Young and W. L. Uglow, entitled "The Iron Ores of Canada, Volume 1, British Columbia and Yukon" (Economic Geology Series No. 3). This report indicates iron ore minerals at fifty-seven localities in British Columbia. These iron ore deposits are dealt with quite fully in this report, and a rough estimate given of the potential tonnage of ore containing more than fifty per cent iron.
In 1930 further geological field work was conducted in the Buttle lake area, Vancouver island.
In 1950 geological survey party, in charge of Dr. J. W. Hoadley, made extensive studies in the vicinity of Zeballos, Vancouver island.
The British Columbia department of mines published a report in 1942 by A. G. McKee and Company, engineers and contractors, of Cleveland, entitled "Report on Proposed Iron and Steel Works."
The geological survey of Canada has no new plans for 1951 dealing specifically with iron ore deposits in British Columbia. However, the field work of Dr. J. W. Hoadley in
the Zeballos area will be continued, and this will include mapping and studies of potential iron deposits.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LOANS TO HOME OWNERS, LOANS ON RENTAL PROPERTY AND RENTAL INSURANCE GUARANTEES

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO LOANS TO HOME OWNERS, LOANS ON RENTAL PROPERTY AND RENTAL INSURANCE GUARANTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the heavy demands the present international situation is imposing and will impose upon the economy of Canada for defence and other measures have made it necessary for the government to give new consideration to the problem of housing in Canada.
Through private endeavour, but also in large part owing to the assistance afforded by the government under the National Housing Act, house construction in Canada since the war has proceeded at an unprecedented rate. In 1947 the number of houses constructed was 79,359. In 1948 the number rose to 81,243. In 1949 the number of houses built was 91,000. In 1950 there was an unprecedented volume of loans under the National Housing Act, and a record number of housing starts. During the year approximately 87,000 housing units were completed but by the end of 1950 there were about 66,000 houses incomplete, which was approximately 8,000 more than were incomplete at the end of 1949.
The government is aware of the continuing need for housing accommodation in Canada, but starts at the 1950 rate are beyond the capacity of the house-building industry under present and foreseen circumstances. Building supply materials, and particularly products of steel, are in short supply, with the result that many builders and owners are unable to complete houses. One of the main problems is to complete houses now under construction, and what the government wishes most to avoid is the starting of a large number of houses which could not be completed.
Since September 1949, additional loans in the amount of one-sixth of the basic loan were being made, provided that the sale price to the home owner was fair and reasonable; but because of rising costs and the previously announced policy of maintaining January 1, 1950, lending values, this provision has become increasingly ineffective. It will be

National Housing Act
recalled that January, 1950, lending values have been maintained in an effort to curb price increases. Effective immediately, therefore, loans under the National Housing Act to home owners will be limited to 80 per cent of lending values prevailing in January, 1950. The effect of this action is that the additional one-sixth provision is suspended. This does not apply to existing commitments. Loans on rental property remain at 80 per cent. Rental insurance guarantees, now on an 85 per cent basis, will, effective immediately, also be computed on an 80 per cent basis.
Although the cost of construction rose about 10 per cent in 1950, the basis of valuation for National Housing Act purposes has not been correspondingly increased. As a result, down-payment requirements have increased in 1950 by the amount by which cost of construction has risen. Without the additional one-sixth, down-payment requirements are greater by about $1,000 on five-room houses and about $1,500 on six-room houses than they would be were this provision effective.
I would emphasize that the building supply situation in certain fields is expected to become more acute than at present, and would urge that builders and home owners consider carefully difficulties which they are likely to encounter on this score before they embark upon building operations. With respect to the current shortage of materials and the use to be made of available supplies, the government will continue to attach a high order of importance to housing and emphasize it to a degree second only to the direct defence program itself.
It is reasonable to expect that the demands for housing will be greatest in those centres where the defence program bears heaviest. With that in minds the whole problem is being kept under constant review, and every effort within the scope of the National Housing Act will be made to see that, of the new housing in 1951, as much as possible will be built in areas where it is most urgently needed.

subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL ADVISORY COUNCIL

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: STATEMENT AS TO ESTABLISHMENT OF NATIONAL ADVISORY COUNCIL
speechtext:
I beg leave to table copies of order in council P.C. 567, dated 1st February, 1951, relating to the establishment of a national advisory council on manpower. In doing so, I wish to make an explanatory statement.
Plans related to the most effective utilization of Canada's present and potential working force, men and women, have been receiving the most careful consideration of the government.
As hon. members know, since the emergency of 1939 Canada has instituted widespread activities under the Unemployment Insurance Act, made possible through amendment to the British North America Act. The unemployment insurance commission now has throughout the country well-organized offices which have a double function- unemployment insurance on the one hand, and employment services on the other.
At the present time nearly every large community in Canada is served by one of these offices, of which there is a total of nearly two hundred. They keep constant and intimate contact with local working forces and employers in industry.
This is illustrated by the fact that the unemployment insurance commission records, kept up to date from week to week, were maintained for a total of over 2,800,000 Canadian workers who were insured under the unemployment insurance commission plan and who were in the labour force at the end of last October. Further, we have records for over four million workers who were insured at one time or another, including the 2,800,000 figure. The national employment offices during the past calendar year have been responsible for nearly 800,000 placements of workers in jobs. To do this, to provide the commission, our research branch in the department and the dominion bureau of statistics with a constant flow of vital information and statistics, these offices keep in the closest touch with their respective regions and communities.
To assist the national employment service and its regional and local offices in its

work, the Unemployment Insurance Act provided for a national employment committee for head office, and similar committees for regional and local employment offices. These have representatives of labour, of employers and of other non-governmental bodies making up the social and the economic life of the nation. These committees have performed and will continue to perform most valuable services to Canada in this field.
Since becoming Minister of Labour I have made appraisal of the up-to-date information on Canada's working force, on the activities in which they work and on the industrial life of Canada generally that comes to the commission's head office, to the Department of Labour and to the bureau of statistics, through this well-integrated network that covers the whole country.
While the demand for workers was less than the supply in all categories, the objective of this machinery has been the mitigation of the hardships of unemployment on the one hand, and seeking to find work for applicants for jobs on the other.
Now, however, when the demand for workers for the armed forces, and for defence industries as well as normal industries, promises to exceed the supply in some categories, I believe the unemployment insurance commission-national employment service machinery I have outlined could continue its present role without interruption and at the same time provide the medium for arranging the maximum voluntary utilization of our manpower during the kind of emergency in which we now find ourselves.
There are many organizations, public bodies and departments of government vitally interested in all these matters, as well as the Minister of Labour, through whom the department and the unemployment insurance commission are responsible to the government: for example, the Department of National Defence, labour unions, defence industries, management, and so on. In this search for the maximum utilization of manpower now under the voluntary system, I believe the government should have available a joint clearing house for the prompt study of month-to-month manpower resources and needs, for the formulation of advice to the Minister of Labour or to the government with respect to these matters, and for the interpretation of resultant plans to workers, to management and indeed to all citizens.
The success of any plans, whether made under present voluntary methods or under more difficult conditions in the future, will depend upon how well they have been formulated in the light of all the facts, and
Manpower
upon how intelligently the opportunities to participate in them are presented to the people of Canada.
Therefore, with the authority of the government, there will be set up immediately, by the order I have just tabled, a national advisory council on manpower, the membership of which will consist of the clerk of the privy council and the deputy minister of labour, who shall be joint chairmen, and such other persons, including the following, as may be appointed, with the approval of the governor in council, by the Minister of Labour, after consultation with the appropriate national organizations:
Four representatives of labour; four representatives of employers; two representatives of agriculture; two representatives of the women of Canada; two representatives of the veterans of Canada; also representatives of the divisions of the government service responsible to the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, the Minister of Finance, the Minister of Fisheries, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Labour, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Resources and Development, the Secretary of State, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the Minister of Veterans Affairs.
The council may, in the discharge of its duties, utilize the services of the unemployment insurance commission and its national employment services, as well as the national regional and local employment advisory committees now operating under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1940.
I would like to state that a representative of this national advisory committee on unemployment will also be a member of the new council.
The duty of the council will be to consider various aspects of manpower questions; to advise on plans under review, and to suggest plans which should be developed so as to make for the most effective utilization in the national interest of the present and potential man and woman working force of Canada.
In organizing this council the government is determined that the greatest care shall be exercised in seeing to it that our available working personnel-particularly in the skilled trades-shall be distributed amongst the armed forces, defence production and civilian activities in the most effective manner possible.
I am informed by the joint chairmen, Mr. Norman Robertson and Mr. Arthur MacNamara, that it is their intention to call the first meeting of the council just as soon as all its members have been appointed, which I hope will be within a week.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my position as a parliamentary adviser to the Canadian delegation, which I have had the honour and privilege of occupying at the fifth general assembly of the United Nations at New York, makes it somewhat imperative that I commence my humble observations on foreign affairs with a word about the structure of the Canadian delegation itself. The multiple-party character and composition of our Canadian representation is a demonstration, in a sense, of the genuine desire of people of all parties in parliament to find, so far as humanly possible, a common voice for Canada at the peace tables of the world. It would be toying with the facts, of course, as this debate has already

shown, to declare that all parties are agreed upon all aspects of Canadian foreign policy. It can properly be said, however, that the presence of representatives of all parties in parliament brings a serious sense of real responsibility to every political group sharing the stirring experience of these United Nations conclaves. Moreover, it provides all parties with the basic considerations and atmospheric background upon which governmental foreign policy is predicated and made.
Unlike our neighbours to the south, who have a type of bi-partisan delegation structure where the Republicans are full-fledged voting delegates, enunciating government policy along with their Democratic colleagues in the assembly deliberations, Canadian opposition representatives are not delegates in that sense of the term. We are parliamentary advisers only. We neither initiate nor assume responsibility for Canadian foreign policy, which, properly, is for the government of the day. Nevertheless we sit in on all delegation deliberations, and are free to participate as fully as we desire. In this way we are left free and unfettered in our constitutional position as critics of the government in both the domestic and the foreign field. It is by far the most sensible and practical arrangement I have seen in the four United Nations meetings in which I have been privileged to play a part.
It is common knowledge that the future of the United Nations organization has been hanging delicately in the balance and largely because it has been compelled to operate under well-nigh impossible conditions. Its failure to impose a durable collective security structure upon the post-war world recalls to our minds at once that it was originally instituted to function in a one-world structure and not in a world split down the centre by two challenging and violently competing ways of life. It was designed to discipline the fretful, the uneasy and the aggressively ambitious state with the collective weight of all the rest. It takes only a casual student of world affairs to see at once that any attempt by almost one-half of the world to discipline the other half under peaceful auspices raises the gravest kind of problems. When one adds to these factors the failure of the victor nations to agree among themselves upon suitable treaties of peace with the vanquished powers and the presence abroad of a poisonous cominform which aims to sap the vitals of and to plant treason behind the lines in all the free nations, and which plans to overthrow with terror, brute strength and hate the very governments which sit with the Soviets around the council tables of the world, it becomes unmistakably clear how far fear, division and distrust have combined with the
The Address-Mr. Graydon abuse of the veto privilege to paralyse [DOT] this adventure into the realm of lasting peace. Nevertheless it is all we have in the world on a global scale where nations can still present their cases, short of resort to arms, and the world is naturally reluctant to abandon it. Perhaps that accounts in part for the stubborn and obdurate fact that not a single one of the sixty nations in the organization has ever withdrawn from membership, while several are on the waiting list anxiously seeking admission. That, in itself, has, in my humble opinion, more than a little collective significance.
I think I must say, after attending United Nations gatherings in various capacities over the last six years, that there is sometimes a little too much stratospheric thinking and not enough of the down-to-earth approach to the problems of the world. For instance, there is a continuing need for realism in dealing with those past masters of realism from behind the iron curtain. They are tough, desperate power gamblers who call for peace on world forums, and, meanwhile, count heavily on the fertile soil of trouble, rebellion, disagreement and chaos to grow their soviet fruit elsewhere. Contrary to Russian professions, I am convinced that settlement of the outstanding inflammatory world issues on any widespread scale is not desired by the architects of Soviet imperialist policy at all. They believe imperial communism flourishes best with the world at the boiling point, and they are doing their best to keep it there. We should not be deluded into thinking that any substantial amount of Russian help is available to reduce the steadily rising global temperature. Their policy thrives on sore spots, and they intend to keep them open and festering. Let us never forget that the underlying policy of Soviet imperialism is world revolution, and its logical successor, world domination. It is hard to settle with people who do not want to settle and who do not think it pays them to settle. That is one of the major reasons why peace stands in jeopardy today.
Not many Canadians relish the prospect of a breach between the free nations and the Chinese people; but the Red leadership of that great power has been consistently waging a campaign of defiance and abuse which in my opinion has deeply injured the cause of peace. For centuries the name of China has stood high in the respect of the world. Her people, with their honest simplicity and pleasant philosophy of life, made friends everywhere. They became good law-abiding citizens wherever they went. These and other kindred considerations have made our diplomatic problems with the new Chinese govern-
74

The Address-Mr. Graydon ment more trying than usual. No doubt the patience, and perhaps the hesitancy, of some powers to put China on the spot and brand her an aggressor and a breaker of the peace can be traced back to the reservoir of good will which exists for the Chinese themselves, but which their Red leaders have been rapidly dissipating. It is too bad that a people like the Chinese have to be judged by leadership of the type we experienced at the security council at Lake Success a few short weeks ago. I watched, as did other members of the Canadian delegation, the unpleasant and hostile demeanour of General Wu, the spokesman for the communist government of China, as he delivered what was virtually an ultimatum in terms of fire, brimstone and vitriol. It was a provocative, abusive and defiant effort. The texture of his entire argument paralleled closely the Muscovite line. It was clear for all to see that Moscow was making the balls and Wu was firing them.
It is probably safe to say that if, with one sweeping gesture made in good faith, the new government of China would throw off the yoke of Soviet imperialism and go it alone, speaking for China and the Chinese people and no one else, the outstanding differences between east and west could be resolved overnight. If the free powers encounter obstacles in finding common ground with China in the days ahead, the cunning and experienced hand of Soviet imperialism will be unable to escape a generous measure of the responsibility.
We in this party will be unable, when the vote is taken, to go along with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in the language of his subamendment, which reads as follows:
We further regret that while Your Excellency's advisers have generally followed a constructive course in relation to the Korean dispute, they have in relation to the resolution branding China as an aggressor supported a course which is premature and unwise at this particular moment, and which should not have been pursued until the methods of peaceful negotiation had been completely exhausted.
When the North Korean communist forces began a full-scale invasion of South Korean territory last June, the conscience of the free world rebelled over such a high-handed and unprovoked act of hostility and armed aggression. The United Nations, very greatly to its credit, promptly took steps to save the South Koreans from disaster. When it became evident, despite the fraudulent attempts made by communist speakers from several nations, including China, to have an innocent world believe that the Chinese troops in Korea were mere volunteers, that the North Korean aggressors-so declared-were being joined by armies of Red China, there was little left


for the United Nations to do but to declare them aggressors too. To have failed to do so would have set up different standards for determining aggression as between powerful nations and smaller powers.
A display of great courage when little nations are involved, and conversely, a demonstration of hesitancy and pussyfooting when big powers are implicated, would have meant that the United Nations was betraying the very principles for which it was instituted. Even-handed justice is a fundamental basis upon which any successful peacekeeping organization must work.
It is perfectly true that the resolution condemning the Chinese aggression in Korea will not necessarily solve either the military or the political problem which sticks out like a sore thumb in the Orient, but its adoption will at least put on record, with an overwhelming majority, the imprint of the conscience of a shocked and startled world which justly refused to tolerate in silence an armed attack on the United Nations forces themselves. To have scores of thousands of hard-fighting troops carrying the United Nations banner in Korea, with the assembly of that organization undecided whether to brand their attackers as aggressors, was a manifestly impossible position in which to leave casualty-stricken troops for any length of time. The air had to be cleared for them as well as for us. The passage of the resolution was delayed quite long enough as it was. The United Nations appears to have profited, at least to this extent, from the experiences gained from the Manchurian and Abyssinian incidents in the days of the old league.
I was suspicious from the start of the North Korean aggression last spring that the Mao government was in behind the scenes egging the North Koreans on, and I would have been surprised also had there not been some rather active encouragement from Russia as well. In plain street terms, all three of them were hoping to get away with it. They were all caught red-handed. What could they have expected as a reward for their planned and calculated attack, not only upon South Korea, but also upon the United Nations itself? The surprising part of the assembly's decision is not the decisive adoption of the resolution but the fact that the patience of the free world held on so long. The purport of the decision is that no nation may expect to have its aggression rewarded by vacillation, appeasement or indecision. Aggressors everywhere know now what they face. That in itself may prove to be a healthy sign for peace.
At a time when great emphasis seems to be laid upon the provocation of earlier days,

The Address-Mr. Graydon
which the Red Chinese are alleged to have suffered at the hands of the United States and other democratic powers, it is perhaps advisable for us to recall that the new Mao administration chose, immediately upon its ascent to power, to make its bed with imperialistic Red Russia, and seems content still to continue to lie in it. They treated Britain's gesture of diplomatic recognition with studied rudeness. They ignored the patient and peace-loving Indians and commenced to invade Tibet while negotiators of that country were travelling to a conclave to discuss Sino-Tibetan problems. While pleading their case before the United Nations in New York, their forces were bearing down on troops carrying the flag of that organization in the Korean peninsula. Their cool and enigmatic reception to the very moderate proposals of the cease-fire committee, amounting almost to a brush-off at certain stages, did not inspire confidence in the new Red Chinese government, even in circles where sympathy and understanding of China were latently waiting for a chance to be displayed in some tangible and helpful form.
Canadians will hope fervently that the free world will continue to leave no stone unturned to bring the Orient and the Occident into peaceful and harmonious relationships. The door to further negotiation must still be left open for an honourable and just settlement. If I were to underline any part of the speech I am making this afternoon, it would be those two sentences. We do not want a war with Asia; we do not want a war with anyone. We want to help Asia. But naturally we want to be certain that we are not assisting in the building of a giant Soviet empire designed to overthrow us and the rest of the world when we are offering the hand of genuine help to peoples who sorely need it. So we say to the Red Chinese government:	Get rid of your Muscovite
masters, and be your own. We can deal with Chinese as Chinese, but their membership in the imperial Soviet family puts unnecessarily high hurdles in front of free democratic assistance. Take those hurdles down and let us work together in peace, harmony and understanding. We all have much to contribute together, but less to contribute alone.
Despite the temptation to place heavy emphasis at the moment on the Korean campaign and the crisis in our relations with the Orient, the concern of the people of the free western world should not be diverted from the principal danger spot of all, Europe itself. There are powerful and convincing reasons why the Soviet imperialists would welcome a wholesale involvement of the free
nations' military strength in the Far East. They are well aware that such involvement would drain the resources of the free powers and weaken their front against Kremlin pressure elsewhere.
Without ignoring here in Canada the strategic necessity of seeing to it that our own defences are adequate to protect our own people from both internal and external dangers, we should not be parties to weakening public opinion on this continent, although there seems to have been a desire to do so in certain quarters; we should not be a party to weakening public opinion as to the necessity, so well recognized when the North Atlantic treaty was signed, for our own defence, of our assisting in the defence of the free nations of western Europe against Soviet designs, pressure and attack. From the Truman declaration down to the Marshall plan for economic and financial aid, and on down to the North Atlantic alliance, the western world has been demonstrating beyond peradventure that it regards Europe as the ultimate strategic area so far as our plans for the containment of Soviet imperialism are concerned.
The safety and security of the central unit of our own commonwealth is inextricably related to such a policy. So is our own. Soviet imperial possession of western Europe would place the United Kingdom in a position of extreme danger-much greater danger than she faced when Hitler held the channel ports; for science has advanced materially since then in the field of rocket bombing and other forms of long-range destruction. The free powers in my opinion must never take their eyes off the Elbe. Better to stop them there than try to stop them at some point closer home. It takes no deep study of military strategy to determine at once what position Canada and the western world would find themselves in if freedom's boundaries were to become the North and South American shores of the Atlantic and Pacific. To use an Eisenhower term, which he used just a day or two ago, our freedom would inevitably wither and vanish. That means our most critical front of freedom is overseas, and we Canadians must fulfil our pledged North Atlantic obligations to the spirit and the letter of the pact, and we must be satisfied with nothing short of our maximum effort to ensure that we play our full part in this integrated challenge to further Soviet designs.
The free nations have talked a lot. They have done some blueprinting of. plans, but there is still an uneasy feeling that somehow we have not come sufficiently to grips with the danger. They have made a start on
76

The Address-Mr. Graydon defending themselves, but the day for all this must make way for the day of quick and effective action. At no stage in our national life did time count more than it does right now. We must all now get down to the grim, practical and costly business of preserving, at all costs, our way of life, which is threatened at every turn by evil forces eager to see the thumb-prints of a police state on the necks of us all. Not long ago no less an authority than General Dwight Eisenhower himself declared that "underpreparedness is as criminal as war itself".
Canada has a reputation to maintain in the campaign for freedom's preservation. She has her own safety and security to consider, as well as the maintenance of the free world in general. To fail to match our rather conspicuous declarations of intentions, made so frequently from international forums, with appropriate action to carry them out, would place us in a ridiculous position in the eyes of the world, and be grossly unfair to our friends and to ourselves. Parliament has a bounden duty to see that Canadian performances measure up to Canadian promises.
The tasks facing Canadians in the diplomatic field are made immeasurably easier when our two major friends, the United States of America and the United Kingdom, are pursuing parallel courses-and as I look' at the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) I realize that no one recognizes that more fully than he. When their courses diverge, our troubles multiply. The recent diversity of views over the problems of the Far East makes it necessary that Canadians use that calm, collected and common sense judgment for which our Canadian people have come to be noted the world over. It should be easy for us to understand the genuine points of view of both, because we are closer to both than any other country in the world.
It is easy to see that Britain's position in the Far East is much more complicated than ours or than that of the United States of America. Her interests, as a people over there, are more intimate with the Orient than those of us over here. It is quite understandable that she wants, if possible, no involvement by the western powers in any widespread conflict between them and the Far East. Hong Kong has been frequently referred to as the New York of the Orient. Britain has it, and while there are unmistakable signs of a communist economic squeeze-play enveloping it, nevertheless the British still have a substantial economic and financial stake in that uneasy section of the globe. Sanctions which would cut off trade with Red China would take on a much more

serious aspect for Britain than for any other major free power, and it is but natural that she wants to avoid them if other acceptable means can be found to penalize Red China for the crime of aggression. Like other nations in the European area, Britain fears the possible involvement of the United States and other free nations in a war with Red China which could conceivably dwindle, diminish and waste the strength of that great republic to the point where it might seriously affect her power to give dynamic and effective leadership to the North Atlantic treaty organization, whose principal emphasis is laid upon the job of containing communism in Europe-and no small job at that. These and other features of the oriental situation bear sympathetic consideration from the United Kingdom point of view.
Nor can we dismiss lightly the critical position of India and Pakistan, our sister members of the commonwealth. Let us make no mistake about that. Whatever may be said of India's judgment in connection with the present United Nations crisis and her relations with Red China, it can never be said that she lacks good faith or peaceful intentions in the pursuance of her policies. The Indian and Pakistani delegations at Lake Success were among the very best and most highly respected delegations there, although I was unable, as were many others, to follow at times some of the policies they advanced and advocated. Their perilous position in oriental politics must be understood1 and appreciated by all of us. Moreover, we must realize that they belong in the very nature of things to that non-communist world bloc of free nations who want no part of a Soviet imperialistic yoke. They are tied to the apron strings of nobody. We, obviously, cannot go along with them on all the issues that divide east and west, but in their desire to give leadership, in their own way, to a crusade for stability and peace in the Far East, they deserve our understanding and sympathy. It may well be that when the present crisis has been resolved and the cornerstone of true peace has been laid finally, the people of the subcontinent of India, which in a sense is the closest common ground between the Far East and ourselves, may be destined to play a part in world peace which will make us all glad1 of our association with them in that family of nations of which all British peoples are so proud.
Having put forward some features of the present world crisis as they appear to affect two sister members of the commonwealth, I desire to comment for a moment on our neighbour to the south, the United States of America. In the February issue of the

Atlantic Monthly, published in the United States, there appears the following concluding paragraph of a commentary on the difficulties experienced by Canadians in their relationship with the United States:
It is one thing for a small nation to follow the leadership of a great power when that leadership is incisive, intelligent, and informed. It is another when the follower begins to feel that the leadership is vacillating, inept, or uninformed. Ottawa has never been particularly awe-struck by General MacArthur. His pronunciamentos plus his something less than omniscient intelligence service has given Ottawa the creeps. Washington's almost cavalier dismissal as sheer bluff of Red China's warning that it would invade Korea if the UN forces invaded the north would not be remembered if it had not been wrong. But what Ottawa resents most of all is Washington's offhand treatment, which is new and strange after years of close co-operation with the Roosevelt administrations.
I have no doubt that some Canadians hold strong views as to how they think the Americans could improve their conduct in the field of world politics. On the other hand some Americans may not see eye to eye with Canadians in their handling of international relations. It seems to me, however, that any widespread surrender on either side of the border to wholesale criticism of each other at the moment could only result in the fouling of our own nest and in giving comfort to an enemy whose cleverness in laying false emphasis has become a feature of its enslaved propaganda.
The headlines of this week end have heralded the observation of Foreign Minister Chou En-lai of China that the United States wants war. We know she doesn't. We know that the prayers of people everywhere on this continent, as elsewhere, are going up nightly that casualty lists on a world scale shall never be published again. No continent has more to gain by peace and more to lose by war than this. That is why peace is our most precious treasure and one we shall not easily give up.
It is no exaggeration to say that the patience of the American people, as well as other peace-seeking nations, has been nearing exhaustion in recent days. They feel that they, along with other free nations, have been bullied and defied by the Reds on varying occasions since the close of the last war. Vivid in their minds are the compulsory absorption of Poland, Roumania, Bulgaria, Albania, Czechoslovakia, Hungary and East Germany into the Soviet orbit. They have not forgotten the Berlin blockade, the indirect attempt to throttle freedom in Italy, and fishing expeditions of the Russians in every troubled political stream in the Orient, together with the ominous stepping-up of the activities of the dreaded cominform all over the world. Just how long a peaceful nation should take, lying down, these defiant
The Address-Mr. Graydon and undisguised steps towards world domination has raised a special question for the United States, ourselves and others. We have answered that question in the only way we could answer it, and that is by meeting fire with fire. Whatever may be the criticism of United States foreign policy, at least it can properly be said that American influence has materially stiffened the backs and the determination of free nations everywhere to stop these stealthy aggressors in their tracks. Before the last war, the free nations ignored aggression until it was too late to stop it short of war. This time that lesson is sinking in, and we see that the way to settle outstanding world issues peacefully is to be able to talk on terms of equality in strength and might with those whose language reeks of force and power.
In the international field, Canada must always make her own decisions. They cannot be made to order for us in some other capital, no matter how friendly that capital may be. Nevertheless in the formulation of our policy we must continue to be guided by the cardinal fact that in a world shrunken as this, where we are all on the doorsteps of every other nation and where our very freedom and liberty are being challenged, we have to work closely integrated with others in the common cause. Canada could not hope to stand alone, but she could fall alone,
In view of the importance attached to an effective pooling of free power strength in the shortest possible time, the screaming need of putting an end, once and for all, to the harmful and dangerous divisions which occur much too frequently between some of the major free nations cannot be too emphatically stressed. Our problems on the military and economic fronts do not appear to offer as many opportunities for division as our problems on the political front. Somehow this area of disagreement must be reduced and more effective policy-making machinery set up by which high-level problems in the political field can be more rapidly and confidently cleared and decided among the government chiefs of the free powers involved.
When I returned from the United Nations general assembly I was flooded with inquiries, particularly from people in my own part of Canada, who anxiously asked: "Does this all mean war, or is there some chance still of peace?". I fancy this question is asked of every member of this house. It is regrettable that so many qualifications must go into the reply. It is possible, I am glad to say, to agree with the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), that "war is not inevitable". But it would be describing the situation with

The Address-Mr. Graydon less than candour if one were to say that peace can come without our doing anything about it. We can only have peace in this disjointed, power-drunk world if this nation and others are prepared to do something about it. A static, negative approach to peace today will only lead to inevitable war.
The evil forces arrayed against us do not and will not understand pleas for peaceful settlement of the outstanding world issues unless those pleas are supported by columns of might and power. The hope I have for peace-and it is by no means a forlorn hope- lies in the possibility that when two worlds finally face each other, both possessing the weapons and the capacity to destroy each other, whatever common sense is still then left in mankind will prevail and that both of them will sit down to a conference table, both of them speaking on equal terms of strength and might, and call quits before they loose upon mankind and themselves the tortures of possible and final annihilation.
The weakness of the free powers is an open invitation to war today, and despite the terrors which new destructive forces of atomic power have struck into the hearts of the masses of the world, it may well be that had this powerful psychological as well as military weapon not been possessed by one of the free powers, there would have been nothing standing between the free nations and the realization of the Soviet dream of empire and domination over us all. It will be our hope, and a prayerful one, that atomic power will always remain in the psychological rather than the military domain. Imperial sovietism has it in its hands to keep it there, and has that responsibility the same as the rest of us.
In my concluding remarks I desire to turn for a moment to the long-range aspect of this determined fight of the free peoples for peace. It concerns our relationship with those hundreds of millions of men, women and children whose life and development have been dwarfed by conditions about which none of us can fail to be deeply concerned. Today they are on the move, and we face the bold, blunt fact that Asia is in the throes of a giant revolution involving well over a third of the world's population. Many of these people have just experienced the travail and pangs of national birth and national independence. They are sensitive, and are feeling their way through a maze of internal and external entanglements. To guide them, Soviet imperialism had held a Red lantern to light their way. They have been told by the cominform that most of their troubles can be traced directly back
tMr. Graydon.]
to a western colonial policy of selfish aggrandizement and economic piracy. With this communist stock-in-trade argument, every effort is made by the Reds to put us in the international doghouse with the people of the Orient.
The Colombo commonwealth plan of economic help for the Far East, and the Truman Point Four program, are both steps in the right direction towards a better understanding, and while some Orientals may still prefer to regard our assistance as a deathbed repentance, we should not give up or despair in a genuine effort to help the free Orient to get on its economic feet. I was convinced as early as the time of the San Francisco conference, and have said it many times in parliament and privately since, that in the long run this country and others similarly privileged cannot hope to remain forever an island of good times, high standards of living and prosperity, in the midst of a raging sea of international backwardness, distress, poverty and suffering. In common parlance, no matter how you look at it, it just doesn't add up.
Moreover, it is crystal clear that the crushing of Soviet imperialism and ultimate victory by the free powers will not necessarily mean that communism itself will have been destroyed. Far from it. Wherever there are swamps and marshes of frustration, misery, social and economic injustice, greed and intolerance, communism will grow, flourish and multiply, in spite of navies, armies, air forces or science's most elaborate gifts to the means of mass destruction. In the final chapter of the struggle between freedom and imperial communism, the scales of victory may well be turned, not by force and power alone, but by a humanitarian approach to our own fellow men of different colour, creed, nationality, philosophy and outlook in the farthest recesses of the globe. It is a basis of permanent peace which, after the current clash has been resolved, must be seriously considered by us all if the free way of life is to survive.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in asking you for the privilege of the floor this afternoon, I do not do so with the conviction that I have a solution to offer for every problem that we face in Canada. I do not do so because of the ability with which I might convey my thoughts to this house, which has just listened to a great address by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon). I do so rather because of the conviction that it is my duty once more to bring to you and to this house a message from the part of Canada from which I come, and to

express some of the views and ideas I hold on problems the solution of which is so vital to the people of Canada.
I assure you that the thoughts which I express to you this afternoon are my own. In nearly fifty years of public life I have always made it a point to say what I think. If sometimes the style has suffered, I hope that sincerity has not been lacking.
In these momentous times I am impressed by the fortunate position of our country in that we have such an able leader with such able colleagues to help us meet the situation which faces us. In the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) we have one who in the last few years has proved himself to be the equal of the greatest statesmen in the world; and I say that advisedly. At his side we have men who took part in the last struggle; they are men of experience who have shown what can be accomplished. If unfortunately this country is again faced with the calamitous events of war, I have full confidence in the leadership we shall have in this country, and I know that confidence is shared by the people of Canada generally.
If I speak mostly of Alberta and of Atha-baska in the remarks which I intend to address to you, it is because I do not quite agree-and I hope I do not get into trouble with you, Mr. Speaker-with the interpretation of the parliamentary rules which we have been following in this country. We mention the name of Bourinot, of May, and of our own Beauchesne. They refer us to Westminster and tell us that once a member is elected for the far-flung constituency of Athabaska, for instance, he is supposed to cease to be a member for that constituency and to become a statesman and a legislator; he is supposed, as a statesman, to consider everything that comes before this house as it affects the whole of the people of this country. But these rules, sir, which are in effect at Westminster apply to a country about the size of my own constituency, and in which 45 million or 50 million people live. They can get together in a short time. It takes only a few hours to travel from one end of the country to the other. How can I, with the best of good will, do that? How can you expect the member for Athabaska, a pioneer himself in that western country, representing a population of pioneer farmers, ranchers, trappers, fishermen and lumbermen, to come down here and call himself a statesman in order to offer solutions to the problems of Canada and of the whole world? No, sir. I deem it my duty to represent, first, the people of my riding of every political faith. I know the house will not object to
The Address*-Mr. Dechene my doing so. I want to say one thing more.
I will say this to the Prime Minister, repeating what I said a few moments ago. Should war again threaten our country, should you and I, sir, again have to face that awful threat, I have full confidence in the policies and the politics of the Prime Minister and the government of this country.
May I say another word along the same line? I have listened once more with great care to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, and once more I was struck with the strength and the ability displayed by the men who have joined the Liberal party from year to year and from election to election.
The other day, picking up a newspaper, I saw that Lionel Conacher had been declared by a committee, well informed and appointed for that purpose, to be the greatest athlete of the past half century. He is a Liberal and a member of this house for Toronto-Trinity.
I turn to my left sometimes and I see the smiling countenance of the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. McDonald), a tough man to meet at any time and in any line of sport, and also a member of the Liberal party. But there are some sentiments of sorrow in the remarks I have to make. In the seat occupied by the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Ward) sat an old old friend of mine. In this country we have no aristocracy except that of the mind and of the heart. We are all equal; there are no classes. But he was one of God's aristocracy. I refer to the late member for Brandon, Mr. Matthews. A gentleman to his fingertips, he had a heart of gold. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, how much of this world's goods he left his family-it is not this world's goods, because the state takes it all today-but I know that he has left them, sir, the greatest heritage of all, the memorial of a fine Canadian and a fine reputation.
I was not as well acquainted with the late member for Queens, Mr. Douglas; but we had a lot of contact because of some personal friends who used to live out west about whom we used to sit and talk. I had accepted an invitation to visit him this coming summer. That is now impossible, but I hope we shall meet in a place where we can talk about all our old friends.
A year ago I sat listening to an address, and sometimes addresses are dreary things to listen to. I relieved the tension by reading a magazine, and there leapt to my eyes a poem, of which I sent a copy to Mr. Matthews, and one to the hon. member for Timiskaming. Today I want to read it to you, and I want to dedicate it to all of my old friends in this
80	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Dechene house who have passed the allotted span of three score years and ten. For instance, I dedicate it to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), the dean of the house; to the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll); to my deskmate, the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McCulloch); to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Little); to the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black); and to the hon. member for St. Henry (Mr. Bonnier). I am sure you will enjoy it, sir, and I ask your permission to place it on record. It reads as follows:
Before we met and you became my friend,
Age was to me a terrible abyss In which all hope, all loveliness, all bliss Were lost forever. Nothing could defend The old from this grim fate. Now, knowing you, Age wears for me a glory and a light;
It is a silvered pinnacle, whose height, Courageously attained, presents a view Which youth nor middle age has looked upon. You have no words to tell me what you see.
But what you are is proof enough for me That sunset may be lovelier than dawn.
Since I met you, age is a promised land Where hope and faith and love walk hand in hand.
The reason I take up your time this afternoon is that on the day that the news of the death of Mr. Matthews came over the radio I had a letter from him. By that time he was gone, but we all recall the generous and kind man that he was. In his letter he said to me: My dear old friend;
I trust this will find you and your good wife enjoying all that is best. I was just doing some filing today and came across something that again appealed to me most strongly. It was your very delightful note sent across the house to me one day containing a little gem of poetry, and it is a gem, entitled, "To an aged friend." Believe me when I say that the poem and the kind thoughtfulness that prompted your sending it over to me is one of my very cherished memories.
I hope, sir, that I can leave this world with the same kind of obituary that I am so pleased to give to my old friend, Matthews.
The other day-I can call him Art Smith now-the hon. member for Calgary West made a memorable address. You heard it, sir.
I have known him for many many years. We used to walk the same paths. I think we parted in 1917. What a wonderful man he is. What a loss to the Conservative party; what a loss to Alberta; what a loss to the whole country that he has found it necessary to resign. Art Smith came from a city which has given many great men to this country, and some others not so good. It was the city of Dr. Brett, later lieutenant governor, the city of A. L. Sifton, the city of Uncle James Reilly, the city of R. C. Edwards of the Calgary Eye Opener, of James Emmett Reilly, of Richard Bedford Bennett, of P. J. Nolan, Pat Burns, and many others. And now 

here is the last of a great generation leaving our midst. As an Albertan, Mr. Speaker, may I express the sincere hope that Art Smith will regain his former health and remain with us for a long, long time.
Mr. Speaker, today we have been throwing bouquets; and before the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) leaves the chamber I should like to make reference to him. On behalf of the people of all parties in Alberta, may I take this opportunity to thank the Prime Minister for having seen fit to give that province representation in his cabinet. It was a generous move, and we so recognize it because we in Alberta have not always been so generous to the Liberal party.
I am the only one left of that little group that stepped out of office in Alberta in 1921. The rest are all gone. The fact that I am the only survivor illustrates the frailty of matters connected with politics. When the Prime Minister now takes into his cabinet a representative from Alberta I know that he is giving proper thought to the people of Alberta, and I have no doubt that in future, because of this recognition, those people will be more generous with him than they have been in the past.
The Prime Minister, in his wisdom, knows well how much the people of my province have contributed to Canada. He knows, too, about our great resources. He knows that in a short time vast quantities of oil will be flowing to the head of the lakes.
A report has been made only recently which indicates that there are vast possibilities in the bituminous tar sands of my constituency. In that area is the greatest reserve of oil and gas to be found anywhere in the world, without exception-and it is right in the middle of that great constituency of Athabaska. I have no doubt that is why the Prime Minister appointed to his cabinet from my province a man with technical training, and one experienced in business.
I am sure that he will prove to be a first-class representative for Alberta, as well as a credit to his province and to the government of which he now forms a part.
May I offer one further word. I would express the view that even in a state of apprehended war we must continue to develop the resources of the country, and particularly the oil resources of Alberta. We must not restrict unduly any activities in the development of our oil reserves, which are so vital in peace, and so much more so in war. No matter what the cost may be, we must go ahead with the development of these great tar sands fields of Alberta. If the provincial government is unable to do

so, then I think it is safe to say that the government of Canada will come to the rescue, so that this great field of power may be developed.
Engineers have shown that these sands can be developed. Only recently an outstanding engineer from New York gave the estimate that at least 250 billion barrels of oil can be taken from the oil-bearing sands of Athabaska.
On one occasion I stated in the house that if either the Kaiser or Hitler had had resources of this kind in Germany, they would not have been permitted to remain undeveloped. Can we believe that they would be left undeveloped in Russia today? All the more reason why we in Canada should carry out the development of these great resources so as to ensure that we and our allies will have this vast supply of motive power, with which any nation can make itself more safe either in time of peace or in war.
It is fitting, sir, that you should now grace the chair of the house. Perhaps it is within your knowledge that I was born in that part of the country you represent. My family were pioneers in the lake St. John area, at a time when the nearest town was seventy-five miles away. But that proved too close when the railway came and they moved to a place in Alberta where the nearest town was one hundred and seventy-five miles away. Before my father died he took advantage of opportunity offered by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, took over a second homestead, and improved and earned title to it in the Peace river country when he was almost eighty years of age.
In my remarks I make special reference to my constituency of Athabaska, because in the last few years nature has not been too kind to us. There have been crop failures. Last year the condition was calamitous. Our crop was frozen, and whatever we had cut remains under the snows of winter today. It was most fortunate, however, that legislation had been passed in the House of Commons, on recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), which permitted some relief for our farmers under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act.
Then, only a few days ago they were made happy by the Prime Minister's declaration resulting from his interview with the Prime Minister of Great Britain, when it was recommended that in connection with the final payment the "have regard" clause be reopened, and that further consideration be given to it by the British cabinet. Knowing the Prime Minister of Canada as we do, we cannot help feeling convinced that he will win his point. I repeat that at this time I am not speaking for the Liberal party, but that
The Address-Mr. Dechene I do speak on behalf of my constituency in saying that I believe the British government will play the game-to use the expression commonly used out in the west-and that our farmers will receive generous treatment, in consideration of the prices they have accepted for their wheat during -the first two years of the contract. I am fully confident that we shall be treated fairly. As an old-timer, with some experience, I believe the people of western Canada may feel confident that reasonable payments will be forthcoming from the operations of the last two years, as a result of the reconsideration to be given by the British government.
I am not going to discuss external affairs. Twice in my life I had to take home to my wife -and to my mother telegrams bearing bad news. I hope this will not happen again. Let us not permit a condition to develop again under which horrible instruments of destruction can flourish. We recall having seen pictures of thousands of refugees, including orphans and women. They had nothing to protect them, and were left homeless because of invasions by their neighbour, bringing about suffering beyond human description.
An old friend from Belgium, who lived near me in Alberta, died recently. He had lived just outside Brussels, in Belgium, in 1914 when the German army marched through-a million and a half of them. He said you could hear the tramp, tramp of their feet, stretching over a week or ten days or two weeks, and that the marching went on ceaselessly. They destroyed everything on their way, ruining the work of ages and generations. This man said that he heard it all the time until he died. The tramping of those soldiers were trampings upon his soul; they tramped on everything he cherished. They tramped on the flag he adored and destroyed everything for which his nation and people had stood for centuries. I hope we shall never see such things again.
I realize that my remarks today may not be very interesting, but as an old man I have confidence in the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) when he says that we shall have peace. God is still in His heaven and He will be there when all the Stalins and Molotovs and Vishinskys have become only memories. He will be there just as He was after the great autocrats and conquerors of history had lain under the dust of centuries. I say to the government that I am convinced that they have behind them the support and backing of the people of this country, that they have the confidence of the people and whatever they believe they may have to do shall be done.

The Address-Mr. Wright

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like first of all to compliment the hon. member who has just resumed his seat upon a very excellent speech. I want to say to him that I agree wholeheartedly in the respects he has paid to deceased members of this house and to the hon. member who has just resigned. Although I number among my friends many hon. members on the other side of the house I still do not think they are sprouting the wings the hon. member seems to indicate they are, any more than I see wings sprouting on hon. members on this side of the house.
With respect to the excellent speech just made by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), I should like to say to him that I agree one hundred per cent on one point, that the real aggressor in the world today is Russia, on whom we should be keeping our eyes. Perhaps in voting for the resolution which was recently passed by the United Nations many delegates failed to realize just who the real aggressor is.
I do not think there has ever been a time since I have been a member of this house when so many people have come to see me in the two weeks before leaving for Ottawa. These people had questions to ask as to the government's intentions with respect to many problems and I should like to name a few of them. One question which was asked, quite frequently was: What are the government's intentions with regard to our Korean forces presently training at Fort Lewis in the United States? What forces have we in Canada for our own protection and to take care of our commitments throughout other areas of the world?
I come from an agricultural constituency in western Canada and another question which I was asked practically every time I went down the street in the little town in which I live was: What are the government's-intentions with regard to the five-year pool? When are they going to make the payments? These people were told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) last fall that payments would be made before the first of the year. Later they were told that they would be made immediately after the first of the year. Now they are told that they may be made in time to provide funds for putting in the crops. Another question asked is: How much is the payment going to be? Is it going to be 25 cents a bushel, 15 cents a bushel or five cents a bushel? We do not seem able to get any idea from the government and I think it is time we had some information.
Another question which was asked practically every time I went into a store was
	,	' [
this: What is the government going to do about the cost of living? A man would say, "Look at this sweater. It is costing me $17.50. Four years ago I was able to buy it for $10. Five years before that I could purchase it for $8. The storekeeper tells me that the next shipment will cost $2.50 more, or $20." What is the government going to do to prevent the rising cost of living?
Our old age pensioners want to know the government's intentions with respect to old age pensions. I am glad the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made the statement he did in answer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) and indicated that it is the intention of the government, immediately the provinces have cleared the way, to bring in the necessary legislation to make old age pensions universal. But that is not going to solve the problem of a great many old age pensioners because it will not increase the basic pension of $40, $42.50 or $50 which the old age pensioners in some provinces are receiving at the present time. It is only by taking action in respect to the cost of 'iving that we are going to be able to solve some of these problems.
I could go on enumerating the questions that were asked. There is one vital matter that concerns western Canada: the intention of the government in connection with freight rates. Are they going to allow another overall increase or is there to be some adjustment of the iniquitous freight rate structure there is at the present time in Canada?
These are questions which the government should have answered in the speech from the throne. When I was asked these questions the only answer I could give was that probably the government would indicate its intentions in the speech from the throne. But in the speech from the throne we found again just a lot of generalities, with very few definite answers to the questions which are in the minds of our people today.
I believe it is time that these questions were answered. If we are to maintain the morale and initiative necessary for an all-out effort at this time, the people must have answers to these questions.
I should like to point out four reasons why we in this group believe that there should be support in the house for the C.C.F. amendment. Just before the vote was taken in the United Nations the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) spoke as follows:
. . . we think the putting of such a resolution at this stage and in this form, when the possibilities of negotiation with the people's government of China are not, in our opinion, completely exhausted, to be premature and unwise.

Yet, despite that statement, a few minutes later the delegation voted for the United States resolution. It seems to me that there must have been some other reason why that action was taken, and in talking with people I find that there seems to be a general opinion that there probably were three reasons why our government and other governments supported the United States resolution. First, it is thought that there was apprehension in the minds of a great many delegates that if the United States amendment was not supported the United States might withdraw from the United Nations. Second, it was thought that there was a possibility that the United States might be lukewarm in its support of the Atlantic pact unless her wishes were met with regard to this resolution.
Third, I think there was a fear that unless support were given at this time it would encourage isolationism in the United States. I do not think these are sound reasons. I think we should have more confidence in the sound judgment and intelligence of our good neighbours to the south than to think that they would have done any of these things if the resolution had not been supported. As a matter of fact I should like to give the house an opinion which I believe was fairly general in the United States a week or ten days before the vote was taken, at a time when it appeared that the United States was not going to be able to obtain support for its resolution. This opinion has to do with the purposes of the United Nations. It is found in the Christian Science Monitor and reads:
Its inability to coerce a major power was even written into its basic structure in the form of the big power veto which, a fact frequently overlooked in discussions, was insisted upon by the American delegation at Dumbarton Oaks and San Francisco just as much as by the Soviet delegation. We ourselves participated in making the United Nations an organization which could not coerce or effectively punish a major power. The demand that it coerce communist China is therefore a demand that it do something which it is not constitutionally built to accomplish. It is a limited instrument. We helped to make it a limited instrument. It is hardly accurate therefore to say that it has failed. It has only failed to do what it never was given the power to do.
I think that is a true statement. It is a statement of fact, and if the United States had had any idea that they would fail to accomplish their purpose in this way I think that other steps would have been taken. Further on in the article it states that the United Nations is not an always available instrument for American purposes.
I think that is a point and one that we should have emphasized by voting against the U.S. resolution. Any time that the United Nations becomes an available instrument of any one of the larger powers then the United
The Address-Mr. Wright Nations is due for extinction. That is the main point of our objections to the Canadian delegation voting for the United States resolution. By so doing, we are playing right into Russia's hands. This is the idea that they have been trying to spread. They have been trying to tell the rest of the world that the United Nations is simply an instrument made available for United States purposes. That fact is one of the main arguments that the Soviet union is using to destroy the United Nations and yet we give them that opportunity.
The second reason why I believe we should not have supported the United States resolution is that we are convinced that the real threat to freedom at this time is not in China but in Russia, and that there is nothing that would please the real aggressor more than to see the western world embroiled in a general conflict in Asia. Look at the position in which the western world finds itself today. Great Britain has twenty-five to thirty per cent of her forces engaged in Malaya or stationed at Hong Kong and Singapore. We find the French with probably fifty per cent of their available forces engaged in Indo-China. The United States and other members of the United Nations have a large proportion of their available forces already engaged in Korea. That is exactly what the real aggressor wants today. He wants to see the forces of the free people of the world engaged in other areas, engaged in the Asiatic area so that they will not be available in Europe where the real threat is.
The third reason why we feel that our amendment should have the support of the house is that it is of little value to declare a nation or an individual an aggressor unless we are prepared to contain or punish them. Indeed it may even encourage them to further acts of violence. There are three types of sanctions: diplomatic, economic and military. Unless we are prepared to go the whole way, unless we are prepared to institute some type of sanction against a nation which we have called an aggressor, it seems to me we are only encouraging aggression in the world.
Can we institute sanctions without becoming further embroiled in Asia? I doubt it. Any form of economic sanction will require some form of military aid to maintain it. Immediately we send ships or other forces to the east to maintain economic sanctions we are in danger of becoming definitely embroiled in a war with China itself.
The fourth reason why I think our amendment should be supported is that there is a strong tide of nationalism sweeping the Asiatic countries at the present time. Action by the United Nations, a majority of whom

The Address-Mr. Wright belong to the western world, against an Asiatic country before every avenue of possible settlement has been explored, can and will have serious repercussions. In my estimation China and Russia are not natural allies. They have several thousand miles of common border. Along that border much of the area is not clearly defined as belonging to either of them. I refer to Outer Mongolia, Manchuria and the islands north of Japan. Given time, it seems to me that an alliance between China and Russia would become very difficult. In moving the resolution at the time that it was moved in the United Nations it seems to me we are doing the one thing that will drive those two countries together and give them what they may consider to be a common enemy.
I am sure that anyone who listened yesterday to the radio report from Lake Success could not but be impressed by the fact that it is now admitted there that any committee set up under the United States resolution to try to negotiate a peaceful settlement of the present dispute has very little chance of success. As a matter of fact there is talk already of setting up an independent committee outside the United Nations to try to negotiate a settlement. It seems to me that is not good. It seems to me that we were premature in our support of the resolution at Lake Success.
I was very pleased to note that reference is made in the speech from the throne to the Colombo conference, and that at that conference discussions and negotiations have taken place with respect to economic aid to the Far East. I am sure it is long overdue. As a matter of fact we should have instituted some form of economic aid to the eastern countries immediately the last war ended. If we had done so we would be in a much stronger position than we are today. When speaking in the house last year, I made two suggestions. I suggested that one of the ways in which we could obtain the good will of the eastern countries was to bring young people from those countries to our universities and to our industries, to give them some training in the methods of the democratic world. I still believe that is a good idea. I still believe that we would obtain more good will in those countries if we were to bring these young people to the North American continent to enter our colleges, our industrial life, our civil service, our co-operatives, to gain a knowledge of all the functions of a democratic society. It would enable them to see the advantages of a democracy. Little is known about these advantages in those eastern areas.
When these young people returned to their own countries they would be messengers of 
good will from the western world. They would be able to assist the people we may send to those countries as a result of the Colombo conference, to institute the reforms which are necessary if the people are to enjoy a better standard of living in that part of the world. I am glad to know there are others who believe in this idea. At the first of this session I believe all the members of the house received an editorial which was published on January 15 in Maclean's magazine. I do not intend to read the whole of the editorial, although it was a good editorial, but I should like to read one paragraph. It states:
For every dollar we must spend to train and maintain our special Korea brigade, we could spend another dollar to train and maintain a special brigade of several thousand doctors. We could send these doctors, at our expense, to fight disease in the parts of the world where many millions live and die without knowing a single day of freedom from disease.
For every shell and bomb we shall create If there is a third world war we could create with greater ultimate profit to ourselves a meal for the mouth of a starving child.
I believe that editorial expresses the sentiments of this group and a great many other people in Canada agree with those sentiments. We should be doing the practical thing by training people to serve in those parts of the world.
That brings me to the second point which I tried to emphasize at the last session, and that is that Canada should be prepared to make an immediate contribution of food to India to aid in alleviating the famine which is now sweeping that country. I have in my hand a copy of the Economic Annalist in which it states:
Total supplies of Canadian wheat for the 1950-51 crop year are 575 million bushels. Exports in 1950-51 may reach 275 million bushels, while about 155 million will be required for domestic use. The 1950 western wheat crop contains abnormally large quantities of low-grade wheat, slightly more than half of the total deliveries being expected to grade No. 5 and lower. Fortunately, the carry-over at July 31, 1950, included a large proportion of high quality wheat and as a result, enough of the mill-able grades should be available to satisfy domestic requirements and to meet this crop year's allocation (approximately 219 million bushels) under the international wheat agreement with a small margin left over for sale outside the agreement. Both the domestic and export markets are expected to absorb significant quantities of low-grade wheat. If these estimates are realized, some 145 million bushels of wheat (mostly low grade) will remain for carryover at July 31, 1951.
In my opinion that is a conservative estimate of what our wheat carry-over will be next August. What excuse can we have for watching people starve when we have upwards of 145 million bushels of surplus wheat in this country? It is true that this 145 million or 150 million bushels which we may

have as a surplus has a large proportion of low-grade wheat in it-probably over half of it will be No. 5 or No. 6. However, No. 5 or No. 6 wheat will still make a flour that will keep the people from starving. It does not make a first-class loaf of bread, but it does make a loaf which the people of India would be glad to have in this emergency. I see no just reason why we should not immediately make this available to India.
There are three ways in which this could be done. First, it could be made available directly by Canada to India. Second, it could be made available through agreements or understandings reached at the Colombo conference. Third, it might be made available through the food and agricultural organization.
I should like to say a word about the food and agricultural organization. At a meeting in Washington a little over a year ago it was suggested that food banks should be set up by this international organization in order to have supplies available for just such an emergency as we find in India. I was sorry that at that conference our Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) did not see fit to support the setting up of these world food banks. They have been requested by the Canadian federation of agriculture and by the international federation of agricultural organization, known as the IFAO. They have been asked for by a great many other organizations in the world.
There are three main food grains: wheat, rice and soybeans. It seems to me that if we are to carry out our obligations to the eastern world, if we are to carry out the promises which we sometimes make, then some international food bank such as was proposed by the food and agriculture organization of the United Nations should be set up. We have not that instrument available to us now. Our Canadian government should therefore immediately offer the government of India at least 50 million bushels of our wheat to be shipped just as quickly as possible, under the difficult situation which exists with regard to transportation and drying of these lower grades of grain.
There is an editorial in Saturday Night which I believe illustrates the point very well. It states:
At the instance of Senator Tom Connally, the request . . .
