That is the request of India for two million tons of wheat, not as a gift, but at a favourable price.
. . . has been pigeonholed, and no secret has been made of the reason for ignoring it: It is that India's views on China are different from those of the United States. Fortunately, the Indians possess a
The Address-Mr. Wright remarkable calm in these matters. They don't explode with indignation: They say "how childish."
It would be nice if Canada were in a position to feel superior about Senator Connally's attitude . But this country has done nothing yet to justify feeling smug. India's need has been explained to the government at Ottawa. Our exportable surplus of high-grade wheat this year is smaller than usual. Most of it has already been contracted for. But we have large quantities of low-grade wheat, so much that we hardly know what to do with it. India is not making fussy distinctions between grades. People with empty bellies are more concerned about nutritional value than about baking qualities.
Within its limited dollar resources the Indian government is prepared to pay some sort of price for the wheat. The Canadian government should be quick and eager to meet them halfway. But we don't feel much confidence that it will.
Now, here is an opportunity for our government to do something that they have been talking about for a long time. I hope it will seize the opportunity to make this wheat available just as quickly as possible. As I have stated before, the fact that it is low grade does not necessarily mean it is not good for human consumption, and will not save many lives in India. It could be shipped through the Pacific ports. It does not have to go out through the great lakes, over which shipment is, of course, impossible at this time. It would mean that our cars that are available in western Canada could be used to advantage in taking that wheat to the Pacific coast from which it could in all likelihood be shipped. It also would provide work for our Canadian mills. Much of this wheat could be crushed in the mills in western Canada and at the Pacific coast and made available in the form of flour to the Indian people at this time.
I want to say a few words with, respect to the situation in which we in western Canada find ourselves today. I do not think the government fully appreciates just what happened in western Canada last fall, and I am certain that hon. members from the east do not. In July we had the prospect of one of the best crops ever harvested in western Canada. Had nothing happened, in all probability we would have harvested a crop of from 550 million to 600 million bushels of wheat last year. But in the latter part of July we had severe frosts. Immediately after those frosts it was announced by the people who made a survey of the situation that our crop was probably reduced by some 65 million bushels. Later that estimate was raised by another 20 million bushels.
But that was not the worst of the situation. Not only was the yield reduced but the grade of the grain was seriously affected. In the west our average grade is usually No. 2. This year it will be No. 4 and No. 5. On top of that we had about one week of good

The Address-Mr. Wright harvesting weather. Then the weather broke and as a result a large share of the western crop, probably 50 per cent of it, was threshed either tough or damp, and much of it was not threshed at all. In my own area-and I think this applies on an average throughout western Canada-15 per cent of the crop is still lying out under a foot of snow, not cut at all, or if it is cut, it is lying in the stook or in the swath. Whether this grain will be harvested or not will depend entirely upon weather conditions next spring.
As to the grain that we were able to thresh, owing to transportation difficulties we have not been able to move it to market. This year a much smaller amount of grain has been moved to market than in any other year. The harvest was late to begin with. Then we found that many of our freight cars were down in the United States although they were needed here for the moving of our harvest. On top of that, we found that we had great difficulty on the great lakes in securing boat space for the movement of grain from Fort William to eastern terminals. The boats were being used mostly by the United States at that time in moving strategic materials. As a result, we had a congestion at the head of the lakes. Consequently probably 50 per cent of our crop is not in a position where any money can be realized on it. If there ever was a time when the farmer in western Canada needed money, it is right now. He needs the final payment on that five-year pool a great deal more now than he needed the 20-cent interim payment which was made before the 1949 election. I can assure the government of that. I do not remember a year in the last several when there have been as many debts left unpaid at the local store and to the local implement dealers as there are today in western Canada. We just have not been able to deliver enough grain to meet our running expenses.
I think the government were wise when they made a further interim payment on this year's crop with respect to wheat and coarse grains. That was a wise move and one that will be appreciated by the farmers in western Canada. Nevertheless, that is not enough. Because of the fact that we have not been able to make our usual deliveries, it is not enough to enable the average farmer to meet the debts which are owed right at the present time to our local people. I would urge on the government that, as soon as possible, they make a substantial final payment on the five-year pool. It is needed now more than it has ever been needed before.
These are things in which we are vitally interested in western Canada. They are matters to which the government should give


immediate attention. Unless they do, we are going to find the position extremely difficult next spring. As to the movement of grain, according to press reports at the present time we are going to have approximately 200 cars a day available from now until navigation opens next spring. What do 200 cars amount to when there are approximately 2,800 delivery points in western Canada? It simply means that we shall get only 2 cars a week at the average delivery point in western Canada for the shipment of grain between now and next spring. That is not enough to meet even the movement of the damp grain that we* find in our bins and in the fields in western Canada; because a great deal of that damp grain that has been threshed has simply been left in the fields. The farmers have not even put it into a granary because they were afraid that if they did so it would heat.
I know that there are difficulties in this matter. I know that the drying facilities at the head of the lakes are being used twenty-four hours a day and that in many cases damp grain, with 20 per cent to 30 per cent moisture content, must be dried not once but two or three times before it can be permanently binned. It seems to me that those drying facilities should be increased or that we should try to see if we cannot obtain some means of using United States drying facilities that might be available south of the line for the purpose of drying some of our grain that we are selling down there. It might be moved down there even when it is tough or damp, dried by means of the United States drying facilities and distributed in the United States market. Every endeavour should be made to get as much as possible of this damp grain moved before the middle of March. Otherwise it is going to spoil in the granaries and on the farms of western Canada, and we shall find that not only shall we have the tremendous losses we have had to date with respect to this year's crop but we shall have further losses owing to the deterioration and the heating of this grain when spring comes.
These are matters which require immediate attention. They are matters which have been brought to the attention of the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, through the farmers' unions and other bodies in western Canada. At their annual meeting in Calgary just recently the Canadian Federation of Agriculture passed a number of resolutions which they have forwarded to the government with the request that they take some action. Among the resolutions was one expressing some dissatisfaction with the working of the federal price support policy. The meeting voted solidly for a resolution asking the federation to try to secure from

Ottawa an adequate statement of policy and implementation of such policy which would assure more active and more general use of the existing price support powers under the Agricultural Prices Support Act which we passed here at the last session. It seems to me that this is action which we should take at this session. We should see that there is some parity price guaranteed to agriculture in western Canada, and throughout the whole of Canada, for the products which we produce on the farm.
I was disappointed in the speech from the throne because there was nothing in it which indicated that the wheat board act might be amended at this session. Along with a great many other people in western Canada, I feel that the wheat board act should be amended at this session to allow the government to take over whatever remains of this year's crop on the 1st of August in 1951 and to make a final settlement with the farmer. If this is not done, and we have a carry-over, such as is suggested in the Economic Annalist, of some 145 million bushels of low-grade wheat it will mean that we shall not be able to dispose of it for probably twelve to eighteen months, and no final settlement can be made on this year's wheat pool until all the crop is disposed of.
If our wheat board act were amended to allow the wheat board to take over what quantities remain on the 1st of August 1951 at a nominal figure, say the average price at which they have been able to sell that wheat during the course of the year, and make a final settlement, I am sure it would be appreciated by western agriculture, and it would mean that the wheat board method of handling the grain would be more popular than it will be if they have to wait for from twelve to eighteen months before a final settlement can be made on the crop.
It is not my intention today to go into other matters mentioned in the speech from the throne. If I had time I should like to discuss the matter of the national mobilization of our resources, and many other matters which are dealt with in the speech from the throne, but opportunity will be provided for that during the session when these matters are under consideration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I greatly enjoyed the speech of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), and I was much interested in the remarks of the speaker who has just taken his seat as regards the assistance which we should have been giving to less favoured lands.
One of the things which always impress me, while projects of this kind are up for discussion, is that never a word is said about
The Address-Mr. Blackmore where the money should come from to pay for all these acts of generosity which we all realize we should be performing toward other countries. I wish that somehow or other it would get into the minds of the responsible people of today that there is the general problem of finding money to do these things that everybody knows could be and ought to be done.
It is my purpose today to devote some attention to price controls. In my judgment, Mr. Speaker, price controls should be applied immediately. Everyone at all familiar with the problem of prices realizes that, involved in that problem, are numerous and baffling difficulties. I have no severe criticism to offer the government. I realize they are in an extremely difficult position, harassed by considerations on every hand which make it extremely hard to make the wise decision. Nevertheless I believe that the policy which I have already suggested is sound.
Those who favoured the removal of controls'-and our Conservative friends were among the leaders in that noble task at the close of the war-believed that production would overtake consumption. It was quite logical to expect that. For some reason or other matters did not work out the way they should have.
Those who now resist the re-imposition of control's believe as well that production will overtake consumption in Canada, and force prices down. That may occur. If the war in Korea fails to expand, as there are some dangers it might expand, then conceivably we might be faced with depressed conditions in this country, if production goes forward as rapidly as it could.
But while we are learning what is going to happen something must be done for the ordinary person right now. There must be relief until production can catch up with consumption.
Even after production catches up with consumption we shall very likely have to have for a time floors and other help to prevent ruinous depression falls in prices of all those commodities the producers of which are not able to defend their prices through limiting production or by price understandings or by some other means. This country faces that grim consideration also, so that merely to break the price structure, with overproduction widespread, is not to find a solution to the problem' which confronts us.
The Social Credit proposals for stabilizing of our prices in a war economy may be summarized as follows: Over-all prices and wages control should be introduced. But at the same time there should be adjustment of prices to

The Address-Mr. Blackmore provide a fair profit, and an adjustment of wages to conform with the adjustment in the price level.
Farm prices should be adjusted to provide for a parity with this adjusted price level to which I have already referred.
Every possible encouragement should be given to increase production of all required goods.
There should be adoption of measures such as consumer subsidies to maintain the purchasing power of low income groups so as to enable them to buy the necessities of life.
Rationing of commodities should be introduced wherever the supply of those commodities cannot be increased to satisfy consumer demands.
As a larger and larger percentage of the production of the nation is diverted to war purposes, thereby making for a scarcity of consumer goods and at the same time requiring an increase in government expenditures, adoption of the following policies is recommended: (1), holding income tax exemptions at present levels; (2), institution of compulsory savings; (3), in the event of an unavoidable increase in taxation, it shall be in the form of direct taxation; (4), any change in indirect taxation should be downward, and any sales tax that remains should be converted to a direct sales tax and advertised as such; (5), if the government is unable to raise sufficient revenue by the above means and finds it desirable to adopt a policy of monetary expansion, then the government should effect that monetary expansion by utilizing the Bank of Canada rather than the chartered banks. In order to deal with a problem such as that of the inflation which now confronts us, it is of the greatest importance tQ analyse carefully the cause of that inflation. Otherwise we may be advocating remedies which would aggravate rather than remedy the situation.
There are several causes of inflation, all of which I do not at this time need to mention. For a few moments may I concentrate on one of them? The one important cause to which, I believe, we must give careful *thought is the increases in the cost of production. We find people advocating far greater taxation in order to draw off purchasing power. I do not see that greater taxation would be of very great value. My fear is that such greater taxation would actually increase costs, and probably do more harm than good.
As an example of how prices have increased through increased production costs, let us consider that in April 1946 the prices


board permitted an increase in the price of pig iron. That was an increase of $5 a ton. I believe that on that occasion I pointed out that it was a dangerous move owing to the fact that iron entered into the construction of so many commodities of great importance. As I recall it, I advocated at that time that, if it were found necessary to give an increase of $5 a ton by way of remuneration to the steel companies, such increase should take the form of a government subsidy, the money to be drawn from the consolidated revenue fund. I am still of the opinion that that procedure should have been adopted.
Just let us think of the vast number of commodities in Canada the production costs of which are directly affected by an increase in the cost of iron and steel. It would be a most impressive list, if it were detailed before the house.
Because of the tremendous number of commodities, the cost of production of which was forced up by the increase in the price of steel, there was both a direct and an indirect effect upon the price of a vastly greater number of commodities. To make matters worse there was a strike of steelworkers in 1946. They said, in effect, "Well, if the steel companies are going to have more money, then we are going to get our share of it." They struck and, if my memory is correct, they remained on strike for eighty-two days, during which time there was tremendous loss of production in the country. This might have been the factor which determined finally that production would not keep pace with or catch up with consumption in this country. At any rate the steelworkers' strike set an example to other workers all across Canada, and a standard from which they could judge their incomes. Either through strikes or through threats of strikes wage increases became impressive, and were made almost all across the board.
I fear these movements were the factors which put the price structure of Canada on the skids. As everyone knows today we see price increases taking place throughout the nation in a completely bewildering fashion. Let us consider for instance the recent increase in the price of bread. Already at this time today some of the bread companies have increased the price of a loaf of bread by one cent, and many others are expecting to follow this example.
I am told by one who I believe is qualified to judge that, even after this present increase is made by the bread companies, they will not be in as favourable a position as they were when they made a similar advance of one cent per loaf during the summer of 1950.

As a result of the advance in 1950, Miss Jean I. Hamilton, corresponding secretary of the Canadian association of consumers in Toronto, wrote to Arthur May, executive secretary of the national council of the baking industry, protesting against that one-cent increase, and expressing the opinion that it was something of an outrage, for which no justification could be shown.
On September 7, 1950, Mr. May wrote a letter in reply to Miss Hamilton. I think the people throughout the country would be interested in reading certain passages from that letter-one which I believe every member of parliament received. It is addressed to Miss Hamilton at 32 Alvin avenue, Toronto, and states:
"I have to acknowledge receipt of your letter of August 29 on the subject of increased prices for ingredients going into the manufacture of bread.
The baking industry has been experiencing cost increases on a continuing and cumulative basis since the beginning of this year. The selling price for one product is, of course, the cost price for those using the product in question, and the increased costs which bakers have experienced reflect in a general way the widespread increases that have occurred in the cost of living.
It is not possible for me to give you details of these cost increases for all the many raw materials and services which bakers employ, but the following represent a few of the more important items:
Lard-The wholesale price of lard has increased since June from 12J cents per pound to 221 cents.
Shortening

The wholesale price of shortening has increased from 26 cents to 32^ cents per pound.
Sugar-Wholesale prices have increased from $8.40 to $9.86 per 100 pounds.
Milk powder-Roller process has increased from 8J cents per pound to 13-14 cents.
Spray process has increased from 10 to 16 cents per pound.
Malt products have increased about one cent per pound.
Raisins have increased from $11.76 per 100 pounds to $14.50.
Salt has increased 33 cents per 100 pounds (arising out of the last freight rate increase).
Shipping cartons have increased (on September 4) by approximately 10 per cent.
Waxed paper has increased in August by approximately 3 per cent."
Today I was speaking with a man prominent in the baking industry who said that since the time that letter was written, September 7, 1950, the increases in costs of these various commodities affecting the cost have been even more striking than they had been up to that time. The letter continues, in another passage:
Further, labour costs have been climbing. It is a fact that those bakers whose shops are unionized invariably experience hourly wage increases and company paid benefits on every contract re-negotiation. Apart from this, bakers are increasing wages and salaries on an individual employee basis continuously. It is difficult to arrive at an estimate
The Address-Mr. Blackmore for increased labour costs, but it is very substantial and certainly not less than the rate of increase which has occurred for raw materials. Nor is the end in sight. I think it is reasonable to assume that there is absolutely no prospect for lower labour costs in the baking industry, and every probability that labour costs will continue to climb.
Finally, mention should1 be made of the cost increases which are manifold and which have occurred for the variety of miscellaneous goods and services which the baking industry require in the manufacture and distribution of their products. Fuel costs are up-both coal and oil have again risen in recent months. Truck replacement and maintenance are up sharply. Truck tires, for example, have been subject to the following increase:	December 7J per cent, May 15 per cent, July 'll per cent and August 20 per cent. A list of all such cost increases would be endless but these two examples are typical.
I should like to quote the final paragraph of the letter, which reads:
I wish I could give the members of your organization assurance that even after the recent increases bread prices would go no higher. Unfortunately, I cannot. If the present inflationary trends continue for raw materials and labour which bakers employ, further price increases will become inevitable. And no one will deplore this more than the baker. The record shows that the sale of bakery products is extremely sensitive to the law of diminishing returns. Higher prices invariably result in lowered sales volume. But bakers are not magicians, and it is beyond their power to continue long to exist if they do not adjust their prices consistent with their costs. Certainly them profit margins have always been, and are today, so small that they simply cannot absorb any substantial measure of further cost increases.
Yours very truly,
National Council of Baking Industry (Signed) Arthur May
For any government agency, any banker, any financier or any economist in Canada to indulge in propaganda in order to try to convince the people of Canada that the cause of these rises in the cost of living is the fact that there is too much money in circulation is for that person to manifest either ignorance or dishonesty.
This is the first thing we have to face. This increase in cost of living has been the result of action by this government right here in Canada in permitting freight rate and other increases. This government has allowed freight rate increases which have resulted in a wide variety of annoying increases in the cost of living and the cost of producing all over Canada-outside of Ontario and Quebec. For the government to pretend that these advances in cost are the result of too much money in circulation I say is to insult the Canadian people and is a downright shame. If we face the facts we will not be talking about the laying on of taxation to draw off surplus purchasing power which is said to be the cause of these enormous increases in prices.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore I will not argue that increased purchasing power in the hands of the people does not have something to do with it.
I do not think it would be wise to go into this matter any further at the present time. Sufficient is contained in that letter to cause us to think. I have given the Social Credit proposals and now I should like to summarize them. We urge that there should be an increase in production to make our country more and more self-supporting. That suggestion has been urged upon the government by a number of agencies, and I think every hon. member knows that such is the case. For example, we have the Canadian Bank of Commerce monthly commercial letter for November, 1950, urging greater production. We have organizations such as the Canadian Manufacturers' Association urging increases in production. Therefore we Social Crediters are not unique in urging this increase in production.
My own feeling has been, and it was during the war, that there are altogether too many annoying taxes and restrictions of various kinds that are interfering with production in the country. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has indicated that he is aware of this and is apparently prepared to clear all such regressive taxation from the statute books of the future. I hope he will be able to do that and not have to yield to the importunities of some group within the cabinet or elsewhere who might urge a different course.
We in Canada are capable of producing many more of the things we need1; in fact we are capable of producing sufficient of most things for our needs. All we have to do is to give our producers encouragement and the guarantee that they will not be destroyed by some change in regulation which will render it impossible for them to sell their product in Canada at a remunerative price. The more nearly we can become independent in the matter of production, the safer we are going to be in the days now coming along.
Second, the Social Credit group urge that little if any increased taxation shall be used to draw off surplus purchasing power. Both of the points I have mentioned are clearly indicated in the list of proposals which I gave at the outset of my speech. There is no need to go into them further.
I repeat, third, we urge that there should be over-all price control with continuous adjustments to make for equity toward all groups, both of producers and consumers.
It is of the first importance in this critical time in our history that every group in this nation shall realize that there is a definite
responsibility on every individual to produce all that can possibly be produced and do everything possible to prevent increased prices. If we cannot get our people to realize the gravity of this fact, then we face perilous times indeed. If we can pull together as a great co-operative union, if we each agree to do our part to make this nation the great powerful factor for stabilization in the world that it is capable of being, then I believe that we have no need for fear of the future supplies of goods and services at prices we all can afford, or with respect to the part we are to play in the powerful dramas which appear about to be enacted all over the world. I hope that all our people, producers and labourers, can come to realize that the more we force up the cost of living the more we endanger this wonderful Canada, so dear to us all.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) have given us the government's view of the present situation and set out the objectives of our country and the prospects for peace. In their endeavours in this connection, as well as in their statements, I feel sure that I voice the views of all hon. members of this house, of all the people of this country as well as a great number of peoples of other countries, when I say that in all those endeavours they made to maintain and preserve peace they had our strong united support.
Our purpose is peace, and it is for this purpose only that the government thinks it right to recommend to this house and to the country these further measures to increase the state of preparedness of ourselves and our allies.
The Canadian government's defence program put before you tonight results directly from the world situation. That program is intended to provide, as Canada's part of an effective deterrent against aggression, what is considered necessary at this time for the defence of Canada against attack and to carry out Canada's undertakings under the charter of the United Nations and the North Atlantic treaty to the full.
Put together, these plans are intended to provide for nearly one hundred ships in the navy, manned and equipped, forty regular and auxiliary squadrons in the air force,
[Mr. Blackmore.l

the equivalent of over a division in the army, and in all three services, administrative and training establishments and equipment and stores which with current production will enable us to meet the shock of mobilization, and all this in addition to furnishing our allies with hundreds of millions of dollars worth of equipment to strengthen their forces in our common defence.
This is a three-year program to involve the expenditure during that period of some $5 billion.
Many times it has been said that war is not inevitable. Neither is peace certain. This large expenditure, almost four times as great as the expenditure voted last year, is felt to be justified as the increased premium to ensure peace. The Canadian government's view is that the chance of maintaining peace will increase as the forces opposed to aggression become stronger. That belief is shared by our eleven allies under the North Atlantic treaty.
Since parliament adjourned on September 15, a great deal has happened to affect the international climate. These developments have been dealt with by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. While no one can clearly penetrate the dark curtain of the uncertain future, most people assume that the risk of a general war is greater than it was when we last met five months ago.
Because of that view, all of the North Atlantic treaty countries have separately and together re-examined the position of their defences.
Canada's defence objectives.-While the situation has changed, the objectives of our foreign policy and of our defence program remain the same.
The object of our foreign policy is to preserve peace and to build up the broad foundations of security which are essential to the prosperity, the welfare and the happiness of our own and other people. In dealing with foreign or defence policy it must never be forgotten that the ultimate object of all our efforts is human welfare. In so far as we can do so consistently with national and international security, we must press forward with everything that will build up the good society here and everywhere else.
The objectives of our national defence are simple and clear. They are: (1) The immediate defence of Canada and North America from direct attack; (2) the implementation of any undertakings made by Canada under the charter of the United Nations, or under the North Atlantic treaty or other agreement for collective security; (3) the organization to build up our strength in a total war.
The Address-Mr. Claxton
Let us examine each of these in turn.
Defence of Canada against direct attack.- As has been said many times, if a war should come, the government believes that the best place to defend Canada would be as far away from our shores as possible. Consequently, everything we do for the collective defence is done for the defence of Canada herself. But to make that possible, we must do what is feasible to make this continent secure from attack.
Russian medium bombers of the B-29 type could reach pretty well any part of North America on a one-way trip and, under certain conditions, reach some parts of North America and return. This being the case, it is quite likely that in a general war Russia would launch bombing attacks against North America either with atomic or conventional weapons.
' There is no way of making a continent of seven million square miles impregnable or impenetrable with a kind of aerial Maginot line. Radar and fighters, combined in a heroic team, won the battle of Britain; but despite the heavy concentration of air defences in that small area, many enemy aircraft got through.
To meet the possibility of air attack, our services are working in close co-operation with the United States. A screen of stations with the latest and most powerful radar apparatus is being built, connected with a network of communications and backed up by squadrons of fighters. The American and Canadian chains will be linked together to form a single system, of which about one-quarter will be in Canada.
If the question is asked why this radar and fighter defence is not already fully operational, it is because the radar, the type of communications selected and the aircraft- the F-86 Sabre and the CF-100 Canuck-have only recently been developed and have not yet been produced in the numbers required. As fast as aircraft can be produced, regular and auxiliary fighter squadrons will be manned and equipped to war strength. In the interim, the R.C.A.F. has mobile radar sets and Vampire and Mustang fighters.
To supplement these air defences the army has a large stock of heavy anti-aircraft guns to be manned by active and reserve force personnel.
In addition to attack by air, it might be possible for an enemy to land airborne troops by a surprise attack on an airfield or by parachute. To meet this possibility the Canadian army has a specially-trained airborne brigade group. For much the same purpose the United States has similar but larger formations. It is noteworthy that none of

The Address-Mr. Claxton these formations was moved to Korea because they were specially trained and earmarked for this particular type of continental defence
In support of the regular forces and to take action to prevent sabotage are the reserve forces as well as the R.C.M.P. and other police.
In continental defence the navy is respon sible for the protection of coastal sea lanes and shipping against enemy action, including mines, and for the vital task of keeping our harbours and approaches open. Ships and installations are being constructed to discharge this role. The R.C.A.F. is building up a number of maritime squadrons for antisubmarine work.
Civil defence.-Because of the possibility of direct attack, it is necessary for us to take precautions for civil defence. Military defence has as its objective the defeat of the enemy and the defence of the country against direct attack. The object of civil defence is to reduce the consequences of enemy action upon civilian population and property.
Because of the immense area of Canada and because of its constitutional structure, civil defence is a matter calling for the close co-operation of federal, provincial and municipal authorities. A large part of civil defence is the result of organizing the manpower and material resources already existing in each community. In the very nature of things the agency for action in civil defence, here as in other countries, must be the local municipal authority. That position was agreed to by the representatives of all the provinces at a conference held here last September.
Following that conference a pamphlet on civil defence organization was issued. It incorporates the main conclusions of our discussions as well as suggestions made by provincial representatives. Civil defence organizations have been set up by most of the provincial governments and many municipalities are taking action. The first staff course is now in progress in Hull. That is a nationwide staff course attended by representatives of all ten provinces. We are arranging for co-ordination of civil defence activities with the United States. Orders are being placed for equipment of various types.
One question of concern is the division of financial responsibility for this special equipment and to deal with this and other matters relating to civil defence co-ordination, the representatives of the provincial governments have been asked to meet here on February 20 if that date is convenient to them.
I come now to the support of the United Nations and North Atlantic treaty. This is the second objective of our national defence.

Action taken by the Canadian armed forces to carry out the objectives of the charter of the United Nations and the North Atlantic treaty must be regarded as action taken for the defence of Canada.
To assist the United Nations forces in Korea Canada sent three destroyers and they have given a good account of themselves. They are being successively replaced by other destroyers.
The 426 heavy transport squadron gave great assistance in the arduous airlift to the Far East.
The Canadian army enlisted 10,000 men for an eighteen months term for the special purpose of carrying out any undertaking by Canada under the charter of the United Nations and the North Atlantic treaty. With 900 men posted from the regular active force they form the Canadian Army special force. Appropriate arrangements will be made for officers and men who wish to do so to become part of the regular force.
One unit of the special force, the second battalion of the Princess Patricias, is in Korea.
The remainder of the special force is continuing its training at Fort Lewis and will be available for service where required.
Western Europe.-Without minimizing the significance of the character of the fighting in Korea, it is the view of this and the other allied governments that the vital centre of our global defence is in western Europe. It was in recognition of this strategic necessity that the North Atlantic treaty was entered into by twelve nations less than two years ago.
North Atlantic treaty organization.-Because of its importance to Canada, it is necessary to deal for a few minutes with the development of the North Atlantic treaty organization.
People are apt to overlook how rapid has been the acceleration that has taken place in the march of events. It was only at the meeting of the council of the North Atlantic treaty organization, held at New York as recently as last September, that the United States gave great leadership in suggesting the establishment in western Europe of an integrated force under a supreme commander. The United States representatives stated that if such a force were created the United States would add substantially to the number of American troops in Europe. This proposal for the first time created the possibility of having in Europe forces strong enough to deter aggression. That was barely five months ago.
You will remember that in the treaty the member nations agreed that an act of aggression against any of them would be an act of aggression against all, to be resisted by all.

The Address-Mr. Claxton
To effect co-ordination under the treaty there was the council of foreign ministers. There were also set up a committee of defence ministers, a committee of finance ministers, a military production and supply board, with numerous subordinate committees, and a committee of deputies of the council. This organization was elaborate enough on the civilian side but it was duplicated on the military side by the military committee of the chiefs of staff of all twelve nations with an executive standing group representing the chiefs of staff of Britain, France and the United States. In addition, there were five regional groups each with corresponding military set-ups. It is not surprising that there has been criticism of this organization as overelaborate, but progress is being made in its simplification.
NATO progress.-At its September meeting the council approved the American suggestions and referred them to the defence ministers.
At Washington in October the defence committee approved a plan for the defence of the five regions of NATO. These are the western European, northern European, southern European, north Atlantic ocean and Canada-United States regions.
The defence plan for the first time set out particulars of the requirements for defence; it showed to what extent those requirements could be met; it also showed the allocations of forces that might be contributed by each of the member nations.
At that meeting agreement was not reached as to the participation of western Germany and this question as well as the creation of the integrated force and the appointment of a supreme commander which were considered to be in part dependent upon it were left to be decided by the defence committee when it reconvened.
Meanwhile, at the request of the defence committee, the rearmament of western Germany was considered by the deputies of the council and the military committee of chiefs of staff at their meeting in London.
These London meetings resulted in agreement, which was approved by the defence committee at a meeting held in Brussels on Monday, December 18. This was followed by a joint meeting of the defence committee and council, and the next day by a meeting of the council. It was a privilege to attend these meetings in a dual capacity, both as Minister of National Defence and as representing my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson).
At the Brussels meeting Canada again raised proposals for streamlining the organization of NATO. The defence production board
was set up with more definite terms of reference to replace the military supply and production board and several other committees.
The terms of reference of the standing group were clarified. There was also established a committee of military representatives of the chiefs of staff of all twelve nations to permit continuous consultation between the standing group and representatives of the chiefs of staff of all the NATO countries.
Canada's remaining proposal that the three ministerial committees be consolidated into a single council, in which the appropriate ministers will represent their governments, is being actively considered.
When criticism is expressed of the organization of NATO it should be remembered that the first meetings to organize the twelve countries for joint defence took place just fifteen months ago.
The accomplishments of the North Atlantic treaty organization to date have been substantial:
(1) The twelve nations have agreed to act together in their common defence; (2) they have set up the organization necessary to combine their common efforts; (3) they have set up an integrated force; (4) they have appointed a supreme commander, who has already visited all the twelve countries, as well as western Germany. Our meeting here a week ago was most satisfactory with that great leader, General Eisenhower, who is now one-twelfth our general; (5) they have prepared plans of joint defence and also requirements of men and materials have been estimated and resources examined; (6) each country has indicated what it will do towards meeting these requirements.
Canada's participation in NATO.-Against this background of the organization established under the North Atlantic treaty, let us look at what Canada is doing.
Following the meeting of the defence committee at Paris in November, 1949, a Canadian offer to train army officers and aircrew for the forces of the other NATO countries was well received and arrangements were worked out under which army officers and aircrew for Belgium, France, Italy, The Netherlands and Norway are now being trained in Canada. Later the United Kingdom expressed a need for such assistance and vacancies having been made available the first British trainees arrived in Canada last month.
A further offering is being made through NATO to increase training facilities considerably.

The Address-Mr. Claxton
These facilities, together with those for training our own aircrew, will provide training for over 3,000 aircrew per year.
This operation will require the opening of additional air stations and recommencing the manufacture in Canada of large numbers of Harvard trainer aircraft and the production of aeroplane engines in this country.
The expense of training aircrew for North Atlantic treaty nations during the fiscal year 1951-52 is estimated at $64,500,000, to apply against the mutual aid appropriation made at the special session.
In addition to training aircrew officers in the numbers mentioned, we have here, now, attending the various staff colleges and other courses in this country officers from Australia, Belgium, France, India, Italy, the Netherlands, Pakistan, Portugal, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Last August Canada offered to NATO the armament and ammunition of U.K. type for a division. In November we were advised by NATO that this equipment should be supplied to the Netherlands. The equipment was overhauled, reconditioned, crated, shipped and delivered before the middle of December.
Negotiations with the United States for the purchase of corresponding American equipment have been completed and we have now offered the equipment for another division in western Europe.
The Canadian army-and I do not think this is realized-has in store or on issue most of the equipment for four divisions, even more of some weapons, and as arrangements are completed for replacement, we propose to offer successively the equipment for several more divisions.
Since there are men trained in Europe waiting for equipment, each division's equipment sent to Europe virtually adds a division's strength of equipped forces to the common deterrent force.
When he was here, General Eisenhower asked if we had 25-pounders we could put in the hands of the Luxembourg artillery regiment which was being raised.	The
following day the cabinet authorized the offer and by Monday evening arrangements had been completed both with Luxembourg and the North Atlantic treaty organization and the guns are waiting for shipment.
Speaking to an informal meeting of congress concerning the result of his tour, General Eisenhower said:
In little Luxembourg I had an unusual experience.
I think you would like to hear about it as illustrating the readiness of the nations today to try to cooperate. They are very small. There are only 300,000 people there. But they set their jaws and

said: "We will have universal military service, with no exemptions." They said, "We are very badly handicapped. We have equipment for one battalion only. What we particularly need is more artillery equipment."
And then General Eisenhower went on to say:
When I stopped in Ottawa I told the Canadians about this trouble, and the Canadians said, "Why, we have some artillery; we can ship it tomorrow." When I got to West Point a few hours later I was greeted with the information that the Canadian government had approved of the transfer, and just left the red tape to me and my staff to look after.
Apparently on this occasion we did not have any red tape here-or at least we gave him that impression.
We are placing an order here in Canada for 50,000 platoon walkie-talkie wireless sets designed in Canada to specifications agreed upon with the United Kingdom and United States and likely to be adopted as standard for all North Atlantic treaty nations. This would be the first article of standard equipment to be so adopted for all twelve nations. The Canadian forces plan to use 5,000, the other 45,000 sets being supplied to the other nations.
Canada is also manufacturing a large number of radar sets for supply to our allies. We expect to be making 155 mm. guns of U.S. pattern. We are at work today on the 3-inch 50-calibre U.S. pattern guns for the U.S. and Canadian navies.
In his statement last week General Eisenhower stressed the importance of equipment. He said this, in his broadcast:
For this purpose the most immediate need of Europe is munitions and equipment.
Every one of the continental nations I visited can rapidly and markedly increase its resistance power if it can be promptly furnished additional supplies of this kind. To fill this need, our loyal neighbour, Canada, with Britain and others, is shouldering part of the load.
We feel, however, that equipment without men is even less useful than men without equipment. For obvious reasons, it is important that all the countries concerned in our collective defence should contribute men as well as equipment to the defence of western Europe. Accordingly we propose, if parliament approves, to place in the integrated force elements of the Canadian army.
The force we propose to send will initially be a brigade group or regimental combat team, and we hope that it may arrive at about the same time as the additional U.S. forces, but this may depend on events in Korea.
Material considerations alone might suggest that there might be greater military value in spending the same amount on equipment for forces already on the spot rather than

on Canadian ground forces; but we and our allies believe that the fact of participation by the Canadian army will show more emphatically than any amount of equipment, welcome though that may be, that we stand together with our allies.
It is hoped that arrangements under discussion will permit us to rotate the men serving abroad at reasonable intervals. It is also planned to keep the numbers of supporting personnel as small as possible. How the tail often outgrows the body is well known to everyone with military experience.
In addition to whatever army forces we have in Europe, our army role in NATO is to provide a strategic reserve.
Canada's most substantial contribution to the planned force in being will be our air force participation. Air power is especially needed. One squadron is already undergoing operational training in England. This squadron is to be joined by two others to form a wing and these squadrons will be made available to the supreme commander.
We plan to have in the integrated force an air division of eleven squadrons at full fighting strength, equipped with F-86E and Canuck aircraft. To support them there will have to be a supply line of reserve aircraft, depots, training establishments, and so on. You can see that the air force participation in the integrated force will require a very large portion of our total defence budget.
The Royal Canadian Navy has an important role in the North Atlantic treaty defence plans. In addition to the defence of our harbours and coasts, the R.C.N. will participate with Britain and the United States in anti-submarine and escort work across the North Atlantic. Plans for the navy will provide the necessary ships of the latest types now under construction or those that we now have in commission or reserve, all rearmed, refitted and recommissioned. In this way we expect to be able to carry out our allotted share of North Atlantic defence with nearly 100 ships equipped and manned.
NATO prospects.-The role of Canada in the North Atlantic treaty organization has now been determined in consultation with the other eleven nations. Canada intends to do everything necessary to carry out that role. The program put forward here includes everything necessary to do that.
We are approaching this common effort in the same spirit as our other partners. We believe that if we all do as much as we can we will be able to build1 up the strength necessary to deter aggression or defeat an enemy. In ground forces or in the air this strength has still to be built up, but there are other
The Address-Mr. Claxton important factors which count in the balance when nations come to weigh their chances, including the atomic bomb and the ability to deliver it.
General Eisenhower had this to say:
In military potential, the free nations have everything they need-natural resources, industrial genius, productive capacity, and great reservoirs of leadership ability. Given the ingredient of morale .-the determination to combine for mutual protection-the military strength necessary will be produced at a speedy pace. With every increase in strength, there will be an upward thrust in morale, an evermounting spiral of confidence and security.
The third objective of our defence efforts is to have the administrative staff, the training establishments, the nucleus of trained officers and N.C.O.'s, the supply depots and everything else needed for mobilization.
Because this has been set down as one of the objectives of our national defence, there have been references to what others have called "the nuclear theory of defence". There isn't any such theory. In every country, the full potential fighting strength of the nation is developed only if war begins.
The Canadian forces have today mobilization plans and administrative and training staffs, supply depots, arms and a good many of the things needed for rapid1 mobilization.
Equipment.-This report indicates something of the size of the equipment program now under way and gaining momentum from day to day.
To meet these requirements a new department of the government, the Department of Defence Production, is being proposed. In the first nine months of the present fiscal year, which ended on December 31, 1950,
80,000	orders were actually placed with industry. During this period orders have been placed with trade and commerce, for the sum of $701 million.
The main items are:
Aircraft, $331 million; ships, $96 million; radar and' wireless, $50 million; clothing and textiles, $35 million; motor vehicles, $50 million; armament, $26 million; construction, $113 million.
In the year before the second world war the Department of National Defence spent $34,432,839, and even during 1939-40 only $125 million. It has been suggested that the position of defence industry today corresponds to what it was about two years after the beginning of the last war but with much greater potential capacity.
Additional orders are being placed for ships, seaward1 defences, electronic devices and wireless, for army equipment of U.S. pattern, for aircraft, including Harvard trainers and engines.
96	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Claxton
As hon. members who visit the plant at Canadair Limited will see tomorrow, new aircraft are beginning to roll oil the production lines.
These large expenditures on equipment are brought about by the staggering cost of modern equipment. Some figures about these costs have already been made public.
A new anti-submarine vessel costs over $8 million; a two-engine fighter, $750,000; a single engine jet interceptor, over $400,000; a new airfield with runways, buildings and equipment, $20 million; a radar station with buildings and equipment, from $3 million to $6 million.
Reference has been made to the equipment we are producing and the men we are training for the North Atlantic treaty nations out of the appropriation of $300 million voted last year. Most of this appropriation has either been already committed or is covered by orders for equipment and plans for services now being arranged for.
Part of our equipment program will be to replace the equipment we are sending to Europe by equipment of U.S. pattern.
Canada has had greater reason than any country to feel strongly about the need for standardization. One obstacle was the large quantities of U.K.-type equipment we already have on issue or in mobilization stores-most of the armament for four divisions.
This equipment was of the kind needed to strengthen the defences of Europe, where there were trained men with empty hands.
It occurred to us that Canada could make a very substantial contribution to collective defence by shipping this equipment to them. This also was the only practical way for us to standardize on U.S. pattern. As related above, the armament for a division has already been shipped. Our offer of 25-pounders to Luxembourg has been accepted. Our offer of another division's equipment is under consideration. The rest will be supplied, including probably a large number of antiaircraft guns, as arrangements are made to replace the equipment by purchase in the United States or production in Canada.
By this means we hope to, first, strengthen the defences of Europe immediately; second, help to keep these forces standardized on U.K.-type equipment; third, expedite standardization of our own forces on U.S. type and, finally, tool up Canadian industry for the production of further equipment of U.S. pattern.
This in itself will' do much to co-ordinate our defence production with the United States. We expect, however, that there will be further development of this character all along the line.
[Mr. Claxton.)

Defence research.-Defence research activity is to be correspondingly increased both to meet the increased needs of the forces and to expedite programs which had been planned for a longer period.
Like all our defence activities, defence research and development is planned and carried out in close co-operation with our allies, including particularly Britain and the United States. Except in so far as it may be required by actual operations, there is no duplication between the work done in the three countries.
Defence research in Canada gives particular emphasis to anti-submarine equipment, antitank weapons, wireless equipment and similar fields in which Canada made a notable contribution during the second world war and in which Canadian scientists and industry have special qualifications.
Construction. - We have already placed orders this year for $113 million worth of construction.
Next year the figure will be more than twice as much, made necessary both for additional operational buildings and living accommodation for the expanding forces.
Today the accommodation for men living in barracks is full to overflowing at every place where accommodation is needed. For every man joining the forces today, additional construction is required. That means about $2,000 per man for construction.
Manpower.-Turning to the vital question of manpower, and womanpower too, three years ago there were in the department and services working full time either as service or civilian personnel a total of 54,000. Today that figure is just short of 90,000, an increase of 67 per cent.
To carry through these plans during the next three years the strengths of the three services should be increased to about 115,000 full-time active service personnel and about
33,000	civilians, the civilians being largely employed in work in the dockyards and shops and on construction. This will be an increase of about the same amount, about 67 per cent above present strength.
Because of the large requirements of the R.C.A.F. not only in building up to its total of 40 regular and auxiliary squadrons, but also in the training services, the R.C.A.F. will, we expect, have more men than the army has today and will be spending nearly as much as the other two services put together.
The strength of the navy will be doubled.
The army will show substantial increases.
During the last six months of 1950 the active forces enlisted, including the special

The Address-Mr. Claxton
force, a total of 17,772 officers and men. Through retirement and discharge there was a total of 2,879, making a net increase of 14,893, an average of 2,482 per month.
During the month of January 1951, officers and men joining totalled 3,354; there was a decrease by retirement or discharges of 830, making a net increase of 2,524.
With a rate anything like that, the over-all requirements of this program should be met by the planned dates with men provided to man the ships, the guns and the aircraft as these are produced.
However, there will be some shortages, which will call for great efforts to overcome.
Meeting these manpower requirements is going to require a big effort and the wholehearted support of all sections of the population.
Summary of program.-Now let me draw together in the most summary form what this program is for each of the three services.
The program envisaged by the government calls for its completion within three years but the job is intended to be carried through just as fast as it can be done.
The program has fifteen main points.
In the navy.-
1.	Nearly 100 ships and many small craft, either new or refitted and newly armed.
2.	Permanent seaward defences of vital harbours.
3.	The shipbuilding industry geared to produce additional ships rapidly.
4.	Administrative and training staffs, depots and stores, for all-out mobilization.
In the army.-
5.	An airborne striking force, anti-aircraft artillery and other units for the defence of Canada against direct attack.
6.	Part of the active army with integrated force under General Eisenhower.
7.	Part of the Canadian forces continuing in the Far East as long as that is necessary.
8.	The administrative staff, training establishments, depots, stores, clothing and equipment to provide for rapid mobilization in a total effort.
9.	Replacement of equipment on issue to active or reserve forces, or in stores, by latest type United States equipment purchased from the United States or made in Canada and our industry in Canada tooled up to make a considerable part of this equipment.
In the air force.-
10.	Forty regular and reserve squadrons with more than 3,000 aircraft additional to those we now have of the types suitable for the purposes intended.
11.	Radar equipment manned and located to provide radar defence integrated with a corresponding United States chain of stations, connected by the necessary communication system and backed by fighters.
12.	In Europe an air division of 11 fighter squadrons, included in the 40.
13.	Airfields, men and equipment to train large numbers of aircrew for ourselves and other countries.
14.	Industry in a position to produce large numbers of the latest types of aircraft needed by the forces of ourselves and others.
15.	Production of quantities of equipment for NATO and training of large numbers of officers to strengthen our common defence by assisting our allies.
If time permitted, sir, I might deal with a number of the other parts of the program which will be put forward during the course of this session, including of course the necessary and proper emphasis on the work of our reserve forces. Tonight I felt it would be the wish of this house, and of the country, that the main lines of the whole program should be set out in a broad way.
This whole program involves an increase in the number of service and civilian personnel employed full time on defence from the present figure of about 90,000 to a total of about 148,000.
That is the program, a large one for a country of 14 million people still involved in developing its natural resources and also facing the task of maintaining essential services over an area of 3} million square miles.
Should it be required, there will be the capacity to expand further rapidly because of the emphasis on training establishments, depots and other essential services.
The cost.-Now, finally, what is the cost?
It is not usual under our system to announce the figures of any estimates before the estimates are tabled by the Minister of Finance, which is usually done after the conclusion of the debate on the address.
But this is not a usual time.
Defence expenditures four years ago were $194 million. This year we appropriated in the original estimate $425 million, and then added in the supplementary estimates $142,200,000, making a total appropriated this year of $567 million, which we expect to spend. Then there was in addition part of the $300 million voted for mutual aid. Next year defence, including mutual aid, will require about $1,600 million.
The three-year program outlined will involve the expenditure, in all matters of the defence of Canada, and our participation in the common effort, of over $5 billion.

The Address-Mr. Pearkes
One point I want to emphasize. The program and the plans I have outlined are all subject to change as the world situation changes.
We in Canada cannot control that situation; ail the nations of the free world cannot control it. We cannot hope to have security unless we are free to adapt our plans and our programs to meet new situations which can -and may-be created at any time by the potential aggressor.
Korea created a new situation and we changed our plans to meet it. It is of vital importance to keep our minds free to make further changes and different plans whenever they are needed.
This report of the government's program should make it clear to every one of the Canadian people that its accomplishment is not going to be an easy task. It means a greatly increased call, indeed a demand, on the armed services themselves and on all the human and material resources of the country. But Canada has always met every challenge and the confident determination to meet the threat of communist expansion will be, and here I am sure I express the feeling of everyone in this house, the dominant feeling of the Canadian people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that there were a certain number of seats vacant on this side of the house when the minister started to make his speech was no indication that there was any lack of interest on the part of members of the official opposition in the subject under discussion nor was it intended in any way as a token of disrespect to the minister. This was the last opportunity we had of saying goodby to a comrade who has meant so much to us and whose advice has been invaluable to the party in which he was such an ornament and to the constituency which he represented. I of course refer to the departure of the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith), who leaves this city this evening.
Like the majority of Canadian citizens, I suppose, I am somewhat mystified and bewildered by the statements which have been made by the ministers of the crown with respect to the international situation. As one reads those statements, one cannot help feeling that here is some conflict of ideas and some uncertainty, even amongst the cabinet ministers, as to the gravity of the present international situation. Speaking for myself, coming as I do from the Pacific coast, from probably the most exposed and the most vulnerable province at the present time and


one in which there is probably less preparation than elsewhere to resist enemy aggression, I am impressed with the gravity and the seriousness of the situation.
Living in British Columbia are a great many retired army men and civil servants who have had long experience with the administration of British affairs in Asian countries. They are familiar with the background of what has been going on in India, in Malaya and in China, and they realize that there is a new awakening of the peoples of Asia such as has not happened for centuries. In the new China they see a nationalism coupled with an imperialistic spirit, a demand amongst the peasants of China, for the first time in centuries, that something be done for China. They realize that there is growing up in that continent a feeling of confidence and a feeling which can perhaps be described as almost a disregard of the powers and principles of the western countries. The feeling of the young Chinese of today, in their communist armies and in their positions of government, is one of great arrogance; and it is of little use talking about the western powers losing face in China today. It would seem that they have lost face, at least temporarily.
But we are not so greatly impressed by the dangers in Asia as to lose sight of the paramount importance of western Europe. It was only a couple of weeks ago that I had the great privilege of spending several hours with Mr. Paul Henri Spaak, the former premier of Belgium. He certainly impressed upon me the dangers in which the people of northwest Europe are living. He also impressed upon me the difficulties that they have of selling to their people the need of having a strong heart and of being prepared to resist communist aggression. One point he stressed was that while the people of France, Belgium, Holland and Luxembourg were prepared to hold the gun and the bayonet, they would do so with much greater heart if they saw United States and Canadian soldiers alongside them.
Judging from the remarks made by the minister tonight, it is obvious that he visualizes Canada's having three objectives in so far as her defence forces are concerned, the first being that of the defence of Canada; the second being that of providing assistance to the United Nations and particularly to the North Atlantic treaty countries; and the third being that of the preparation for total war. For one who has risen in this house, year after year, and stressed the importance of Canada's being ready to defend her own shores, it was encouraging to hear the minister recognize the importance of that task for our defence forces. In the past we have

The Address-Mr. Pearkes
heard that the only danger facing Canada is that of some diversionary raid. I have never subscribed to that theory. I have always believed it was possible for enemy bombers- we have a range of forty-five hundred miles -to carry out upon the cities of this country raids of a far more substantial nature than those that might be classed as diversionary. I am encouraged to hear the minister admit that such a danger does exist and that he places as the number one requisite for our defence forces the need of protecting the cities of this country against such raids. As he said, the B-29's of the Russian air force are capable of attacking the majority of the cities of Canada, particularly if they are prepared to carry out refuelling operations in the air en route, which it is perfectly possible for them to do.
The second requirement that he mentioned was that of supplying forces to the North Atlantic treaty nations. He mentioned a modest contribution of armed forces; in so far as the army is concerned a brigade group or regimental combat team. As he said, they might be sent to Europe in the immediate future. Then he just touched upon the steps which would be taken to prepare for the total war if in our lifetime we are to be faced with a third world war.
To meet all these requirements it will be necessary, as the minister said, to provide a great deal of money, and to provide a very considerable expansion of the actual number of serving soldiers, sailors and airmen. The minister adroitly skated around the question as to how he was going to raise the men to provide for this necessary expansion. The other day the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) told us how he was not going to raise these forces at the present time. I suppose if the Prime Minister was in a generous mood he would probably describe me as being one of those sincere and patriotic personages who might advocate other and more positive methods of raising those particular forces to meet the requirements.
I realize that the government is responsible for the method that it adopts in order to meet this situation. I have no hesitation in saying that I believe I am sincere and patriotic; and because the responsibility rests upon the government, and even though I might hold different views as to the methods by which these forces should be raised, I think it would be detrimental at this time to advocate strongly methods which the government is not prepared to follow, because I believe it is of paramount importance that the government raise the men that it requires, and the government alone will say by what method it will raise those men. I for one would be loath to utter a word which would discourage 80709-7 j
any man from joining those forces, or in any way put any hindrance in the way of the national effort carried out by the methods recommended by the government to meet what I consider to be a grave situation.
It would, however, seem to me only common prudence that the government should at this time set up the machinery which may be necessary to accelerate its method of enlistment, its method of assigning the manpower of the country to the various services and to industry, agriculture, transport and all the rest of it. If these steps are left to the eleventh hour I feel that it will not be possible to take full advantage of the resources of this country, both in manpower and in materials. Therefore I feel there is no time to be lost in carrying out a review both of our assets and of our deficiencies. I feel that that review should be carried out at once so that the government will be in a position to change its present method of providing for the expansion which has been indicated, should the methods that it proposes to follow immediately fail, or should the situation deteriorate to such an extent that other methods would have to be followed. There is no time to be lost in making the preparations and in setting up the machinery so that a more vigorous system of supplying the material and the personnel for expansion can be followed, and to set up this machinery there are many requirements. For instance, during this winter we have seen the necessity of sending the brigade which is being organized for Korea to a foreign country, to the United States, in order to carry out its training. That brigade has gone to Fort Lewis in Washington, chiefly I understand because no camps were available in this country where
10,000	men could be trained.
The camp at Fort Lewis was vacated only a very short time before the Canadian troops arrived there. It was vacated by the second United States division which had gone overseas to Korea, and so this camp was available. It is essentially a staging camp. It could hardly be described as an ideal training camp. It is certainly not an ideal training camp for a theatre of war such as Korea. It is a flat gravel plain, heavily wooded, having an extent of some 100,000 acres. There is no opportunity for the troops to train in mountain warfare, and the Korean theatre of war is one in which there are mountain ranges and barren hills, no heavily wooded, flat plains.
There is no opportunity at Fort Lewis for combined training to the extent that companies or battalions would be able to carry out field firing exercises with all the supporting arms such as anti-tank weapons and field
100	HOUSE OF
' The Address-Mr. Pearkes artillery. Actually the field artillery of that brigade group had to go to Yakima, 180 miles away from Fort Lewis, in order to carry out their firing practices. They have just returned. They can carry out exercises with their infantry only of a most elementary nature, firing down what might toe described as a rifle range, so that their own artillery mounted on a rise can fire in a very restricted area.
I believe therefore that the provision of camps is one of the most essential features in any plan to take care of the expansion of our army. The need for more instructors is of paramount importance. Second battalions of the Royal Canadian regiment, the Princess Patricias and the Royal 22nd regiment were trained and supplied with instructors, in the main, from their first battalions. The third battalions of those regiments, which are also in training at Fort Lewis, had to obtain their instructors from the A. & T. staffs of the reserve army. Today they are very short of instructors.
Then, there are more elementary things, such as uniform attestation papers among the three services, and all the need for co-ordinating the manpower effort between those. Finally there is the urgent need of impressing upon all services the importance of thorough medical examination before the men are enlisted. Anyone who has had any experience with veterans' affairs in the last few years will realize how many men there are who are receiving a pension today on account of preenlistment disabilities aggravated by war service in the last world war. Today Canada is paying pensions to thousands of men who had pre-enlistment conditions which were aggravated by their service overseas. In the recruitment of the Korean force there was the same urge to bring units up to strength, and the same lack of facilities for medical examination which was so clearly marked at the beginning of the second world war.
I am not suggesting for one moment that all those pensioners who today draw pensions for pre-enlistment conditions aggravated by service would not have been taken. Of course you would have taken a chance with some of them. Yet, there are a great many who would never have been taken into the Canadian army in the early days of the second world war had there been proper facilities for carrying out more thorough medical examination.
If we are visualizing further expansion, such as the minister has told us we may expect-and such as it is quite obvious we must expect-then I urge upon him that we


should take the preliminary step necessary to ensure that these conditions can be carried out most effectively.
So far as the Korean force is concerned, there are today hundreds of men who were enlisted but who have since been discharged because it has been found that they did not measure up to the physical standards required, although they had been originally accepted.
I said earlier that I realize it is the government's responsibility to apply the methods it endorses in order to bring about the expansion indicated, and that I had no intention whatever of trying to put forward alternative means, and of stressing those means. I believe that in so doing we might retard the national effort. However, I intend to make one or two suggestions which I trust may be of some help to the minister who has to bear this grave responsibility.
I am encouraged in this because in the past I have made certain suggestions in the house. I could not help noticing that, perhaps after a lapse of many months, they have been adopted. One of the most recent was that of appointing an over-all chief of staff, a procedure I advocated with some force in the house some two years ago. I have already mentioned that I had called attention to the fact that some of our cities were in danger. Also at one time I stressed the fact that it was regrettable that we had allowed our women's division to cease functioning, and that there was an opportunity to utilize it.
All these things are now being put into effect. While I am not naive enough to believe that I was the only one who recommended those steps, or that I am the only person advocating those points I shall mention from now on, I take courage from the results which have been achieved in the past.
It was my good fortune to be in the state of Washington on January 25 and 26, just a few days before the opening of the session. I took the opportunity at that time of asking the commander of the Canadian special brigade if he would permit me to see the progress the troops were making, and to get some idea as to the efficiency of those units, and the state of their training. I received a most cordial invitation from Brigadier Rockingham, and received every courtesy from him and his staff, and from the commanding officers of the various units at Fort Lewis.
