I want to say, without the slightest doubt or uncertainty in the matter, that in the person of the commander of that brigade Canada has a man in whom we can place great confidence, and one who is supported by a group of young staff officers who are well educated

in the military art, who are keen and conscientious; that he has commanding officers of the five battalions and supporting units that I saw who have great personalities and powers of command; and that the Canadian people have there units which are a first-class cross-section of young Canadian manhood, who are physically content, who are interested in their work and who can be entirely relied upon to do a first-class job, no matter where ultimately they may be sent.
The special Korean brigade is one of which I feel Canada might well be proud. As a "has been" soldier I would say that they are making excellent progress in their training and have taken every advantage of the opportunities that are available to them to weld together men who before enlistment had few interests in common and who were not necessarily drawn from any particular area of Canada or from any particular class. Essentially they were Canadians who were inspired by a spirit of adventure and who were determined to do the job for which the Canadian taxpayer was paying them.
There were United States troops under training in that same camp. They were replacements, or as we would say reinforcements, for the United States second division. They were reservists, men from the National Guard. When those men took their discharge after world war II they volunteered to have their names placed on the reserve list and if opportunity presented to do a certain amount of training which would be comparable to the training carried on in our reserve units.
These United States replacements were being put through an eighteen-day intensive refresher course and then, because of the need for men, were being sent direct to Korea. I hope the day will never come when Canadians will have to be sent into a theatre of war with only an eighteen-day refresher course. The one thing which impressed itself upon my mind more than anything else was that the United States because of unpreparedness was forced to send replacements to a division which had suffered heavy casualties with only an eighteen-day refresher course.
This refresher course was carried on in a mass production style with an instructor standing up on a platform and giving the details of some drill to hundreds of men. There was no personal instruction, or very little, given during those courses. If at times some people in Canada are apt to criticize the tactics or strategy of General MacArthur I ask them to remember the picture that I saw of those United States soldiers, ex-G.I.'s of five years ago, being sent to join their
The Address-Mr. Pearkes units in Korea after being given only eighteen days of training.
If we say that certain elements of the United States army have not fought to the bitter end in Korea, if we say that they have given ground too quickly, let us remember that the tactics of today are different from the tactics of the Ypres salient or the Somme or Passchendaele, when we contested, rightly or wrongly, every yard of ground. It is a broad question whether it would be wise to fight to the death for each barren hill in Korea. Let us remember the mixed forces that General MacArthur has under his command and that many of the soldiers of his own United States army have had very little training and that units of his army have been rather hastily collected together.
Now let us look at the other side of the camp where our Canadian brigade had been in training. That brigade had been fortunate enough to have many weeks available for training. I saw fire and movement exercises being carried out by infantry battalions. I saw the second battalion of the Royal 22nd regiment carrying out exercises from a bivouac camp. I saw anti-tank units on manoeuvres. It struck me that those units were following the pattern which had been drawn up by British armies and adhered to for centuries.
It seemed to me that the main difference between the Canadian and United States method was that the United States taught their men in the shortest possible time how to fire the particular weapon with which they were to be armed while the Canadian commanders were teaching their soldiers how to fire their weapons from the most advantageous piece of ground available so that their lives might be saved, so that they would not be expended in the first battle in which they were engaged.
It seemed to me that that was in accordance with the British tradition. All through the centuries British armies have been relatively small and British commanders have had to emphasize the importance of preserving the lives of their men. I hope that that will be the tradition of Canadian commanders in the future.
We might say, therefore, that on one side of the camp there was the urgent need of sending men into a theatre of war no matter how little training they had while on the other side there was thorough training going on which would enable the Canadian units to give a good account of themselves in battle at the least expense as far as lives were concerned.
At the present time we are in ,the position of having to change our armament from the

The Address-Mr. Pearkes British to United States type. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) told us this afternoon that we were sending great quantities of arms to the armies of western Europe. Obviously those guns and rifles must be replaced by arms and equipment manufactured on this continent. I do not think that anybody will quarrel with that policy. However, I plead most earnestly at this time that we do not follow slavishly the organization of the United States armed forces, that we do not adopt, lock, stock and barrel, the United States staff organization and the organization of their armies.
I think that any attempt to Americanize the Canadian army one hundred per cent would be viewed with dismay by the Canadian people as a whole. I am disturbed by statements that have appeared in the press within the last ten days indicating that there is a tendency to go further than is necessary in Americanizing our Canadian forces. A wholesale change at the present time would disrupt the Canadian army. So far as the infantry is concerned, it would mean that battalions of old historic regiments would lose their identity. We would have to make a complete change in our supply system. The Royal Canadian Army Service Corps would have to assume the functions of a transportation corps and quartermaster's corps in order to conform with the organization of the United States army. The Royal Canadian Ordnance Corps and the R.C.E.M.E. would be changed beyond all recognition.
Within our divisions we should have to adopt the United States system of medical services, and I think that few who have had any experience with the two systems would question that the Canadian system is superior within divisions so far as medical services are concerned. Surely the care of the wounded is one of the prime considerations of any army organization. So far as staff is concerned, we should have to adopt the United States G-l, G-2, G-3 and G-4 system instead of having a division between our general staff and administrative staff.
Coming to the higher level, in the United States army the corps has very little administrative authority over the division. If it so happened that a Canadian corps was serving with the United States army and we were organized according to their system you would find that our Canadian divisions would be administered directly from United States army headquarters. I emphasize this point because of the reports that have been circulated, and I say that any sweeping changes in our organization would be unwise and detrimental at the present time.
There will have to be minor changes. It is necessary that we accept United States


arms and equipment. If we carry United States arms then it is necessary to modify our tactics in order to make the fullest use of such arms; but with the exception of the fact that we are to be supplied by a United States pipe line I feel that no other changes should be necessary.
Finally, in comparing the two methods of training, while I realize how unacceptable it would be to the Canadian people to have our soldiers trained in eighteen days and then sent overseas, I feel that if we are to face up to the conditions of modern warfare somehow or other we must devise a system of training which will make men fit for service in a shorter period than is now allowed. I presume that the majority of commanders would say that they require at least twelve months in order to place a brigade in the field ready for action. There must be some halfway mark between the eighteen-day and the twelve-month systems of training. The way modern war is fought we may not be masters of our own destiny. As a matter of fact Russia is calling the shots and we may not have twelve months to prepare our troops of war. Therefore I suggest to the minister that he instruct his staff to consider most seriously some method of speeding up the training of our troops.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) referred to civil defence and the fact that a staff course was being conducted at the present time. He also referred to the difficulty of defining where the financial responsibility should rest so far as the dominion, provincial and municipal governments are concerned. We shall never make any real progress until that is settled and the provinces and municipalities know exactly how much of the burden is going to be borne by the federal government and what their share will be.
I throw out a final suggestion, and I do not know whether the minister will like it. In preparing for the active defence of this country he is carrying such a burden that I think he might be well advised to place civil defence under another minister.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister most sincerely for his statement of February 1, 1951, on conscription. I quote:
We know that the cost to us of maintaining one man on European soil, as part of the integrated army, is much more than the cost to the Europeans themselves of maintaining and equipping one man there. And we know that, in the production of equipment, we can get for every dollar expended as much as can be got from any dollar expended anywhere in the world, and perhaps more. We believe,

as General Eisenhower is reported to have submitted in his report to congress today, that the big need of western Europe at this time is for arms rather than for troops.
The Prime Minister did not commit himself for the future and, to me, his frank and sincere way of dealing with a question is far better than what we had been accustomed to in the recent past.
In my opinion, it would be much wiser to organize our own territorial defence and to let Europe raise a European army. We could however undertake to make maximum use of our natural resources and of the productive capacity of our industry to supply the equipment necessary for the efficient operation of the army shortly to be set up in Europe under the command of General Eisenhower.
I even think it might be advisable not to send any troops to Europe or to Korea, so as to ensure the maximum amount of productive capacity of our farms and industry. Our country has only a small population of some 15 million scattered over a territory as large as Europe. If we want to transform Canada into an arsenal and a bread-basket to supply the necessary munitions and foodstuffs to the European army, it would seem foolish to deprive ourselves of a part of our people, especially if we compare our population with that of the United States or of European countries party to the North Atlantic pact. Indeed, the government itself has admitted our shortage of manpower by stating its willingness to supply funds to bring some 150,000 European immigrants to this country. Obviously, Canadians do not like to be compelled to go to the defence of Europe while their places are being taken here by Europeans. It therefore seems unwise to send Canadian soldiers to Europe-at a cost which even the government considers excessive-in order that they might replace those immigrants.
Furthermore a force such as that made up of volunteers would necessarily find itself compelled, in case of war, to replace its casualties with conscripts. I may state with the utmost assurance that if public opinion is prepared for any sacrifice for the defence of our territory, it surely would not accept conscription for overseas service because it bears in mind the tremendous number of people in France, England, Belgium, Spain, Germany, Holland and Italy who, I am sure, want only the necessary weapons to raise
The Address-Mr. LaCroix their own forces in order to be able to fight communists in Europe. Besides, any other course would tend to lower the efficiency of the very limited population of Canada in the development of our vast natural resources, which we could put at the disposal of this European army.
Those who launched a campaign in favour of compulsory military service are being less helpful than they think to the defence of Canada against communist aggression. Canada today can be of much greater service to her allies by helping to set up a tremendous military machine, through the work of her farmers and her workers, than by sending forces to Europe, Korea or elsewhere. Campaigns in favour of conscription for service overseas can only be detrimental to the organization of our own defence. Let us not forget that, if war breaks out, our own country will at once be attacked from the Pacific and we shall certainly not be able to bring back our soldiers from Europe or Korea in time to face the music.
The campaign in favour of conscription for overseas service is bound to hurt our country by causing internal dissensions at a time when all our efforts, both military and diplomatic, must be combined if we are to face that dictator from Moscow.
Fortunately, in these dark and trying days, Canada's affairs are directed by a man, the Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent, whose characteristics of honesty, courage, and vision, vitally important for the safety of our nation, are acknowledged the world over. For goodness' sake, let us not play into the hands of our enemy by dividing our country.
Another point I wish to raise in connection with our domestic policy is the steadily rising cost of living. The government hinted in the speech from the throne that price controls are going to be established in the near future. Of course, there are serious disadvantages to this method of fighting inflation, but it is of indisputable value, when compared with the profit motive of certain monopolies that, in this country more than in any other, control the purchase, the distribution and the sale of daily essentials. Those monopolies strangely help the propaganda of communists, who turn them to account in order to convince the popular masses that in no other country in the world is wealth more unevenly distributed than in Canada and the United States.
In France, and in Europe in general, there are innumerable small shopkeepers and small manufacturers, the inevitable consequence of wise legislation; whereas in our country, we

The Address-Mr. LaCroix have to put up with a monopoly that controls the distribution of milk and its by-products, a monopoly of meat, directed by Canada Packers and Swift's; we have to pay the prices set by chain stores, those of milled feed set by the large milling companies, to say nothing of the monopolies controlling essential public utilities such as telephone, transportation, power companies, et cetera. In other words our legislation is admirably suited to the organization of cartels.
I might, while I am on the subject, thank the government for having recently instituted a commission to recommend such changes as are necessary in our legislation to deal with trusts. I hope this will finally prevent these exploiters of human suffering from causing further harm.
I insist upon the re-establishment < f price control since it has been established beyond all doubt that, between 1941 and 1946, the cost of living index only rose five points while, on the other hand, after controls had been lifted, that is between 1946 and November 1950, it rose fifty points.
May I suggest however that the government change the practice it followed in 1941 to 1946 of appointing as price controllers officers of those big companies that constitute the monopolies I just mentioned. Those men, who were being handsomely paid by their companies could surely not serve two masters at the same time. Could we not establish a more flexible organization, one better adapted to special conditions and able to consider particular cases? I sincerely believe that an arbitration commission on prices, with no representatives from the monopolies controlling our economic activities, would be in a position to give to the public sufficient gar-antees of honesty and disinterestedness. This formula, indeed, is one that is advocated by trade unions. Labour would surely approve of it.
To show the control exerted by monopolies on our economic system, let me mention the case of the Bell Telephone, which has just been allowed by the board of transport commissioners to increase rates up to 135 per cent in the district of Quebec. I now quote the following excerpt from section 52 of the Railway Act, chapter 170 of the Revised Statutes of Canada:
The Governor in Council may at any time, in his discretion, either upon petition of any party, person or company interested, or of his own motion, and

without any petition or application, vary or rescind any order, decision, rule or regulation of the board, whether such order or decision is made inter partes or otherwise, and whether such regulation is general or limited in its scope or application; and any order which the Governor in Council with respect thereto shall be binding upon the board and upon all parties.
In view of this section, after the board's decision, I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) on November 20, 1950 the letter which I now quote:
My dear Minister,
The people of the district of Quebec have taken due note of the board of transport commissioners' decision which, according to the statement of its deputy chief commissioner, Mr. A. Sylvestre, authorizes an increase of up to 135 per cent in telephone rates applying to the district of Quebec.
As you know, parliament has the right to appeal from this decision to the cabinet. I strongly protest against this judgment of the board of transport commissioners because, throughout the examination of the Bell Telephone Company's application, that body refused to accept any evidence showing the relation that might exist between the Bell Telephone Company of Canada and the Northern Electric Company Limited from which the former firm buys all its equipment without even asking for tenders.
If the board of transport commissioners had allowed the evidence of financial ties between the Bell Telephone and the Northern Electric Co., it would have been easy to prove that part of the Bell Telephone profits, through the channel of equipment purchases, go to the Northern Electric Co., Ltd. whose shares, were they quoted on the market, would reach an astronomical figure.
I have already proven in the House of Commons that the ten or so shareholders of the Northern Electric Co. are also the principal directors and shareholders of the Bell Telephone, and as far as I know, that proof I have given parliament has never been challenged.
That siphoning of Bell Telephone profits into the Northern Electric Co.'s till deprives the Bell shareholders of profits that belong to them and the customers of rates that would be set according to the company's real profits.
To establish the cost of the equipment provided by the Northern Electric Co., it would have been necessary for the commissioners to allow as evidence the profits made by that company. But all such evidence was entirely rejected by the board of transport commissioners.
You know as well as I do, sir, that the Bell Telephone in this country is a monopoly of this indispensable service called the "telephone apparatus" and I feel it is my duty to ask you to reconsider this decision of the board of transport commissioners which affects particularly the electors of the Quebec district who are represented in Ottawa by the Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent. The matter will no doubt crop up again during the next session and as the increase is announced for January 1, 1951, and the session will not begin before February, it seems to me that the cabinet should reconsider this matter immediately.

I am enclosing herewith an editorial published in L'Evenement, November 17 issue, and in the Soleil of November 19. The Soleil calls itself the "Liberal organ" in Quebec. Therefore you should not brush aside their views which, besides, are shared by the whole population of the Quebec district.
I am sending today a copy of this letter to the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent and I rely on your kindness, since the board of transport commissioners are responsible to you, to take the necessary steps to defer the enforcement of that ruling and leave it to parliament to decide.
On December 4, 1950, the Minister of Transport replied as follows:
My attention was called, upon my return, to your letter of November 20 about the decision of the board of transport commissioners approving the revision of certain rates of the Bell Telephone Company in the district of Quebec.
As you know, the Bell Company's request for a general increase of their rates was considered by the board of transport commissioners during an investigation which began on March 8, 1950, and was completed on June 2 last. Following that investigation, the board ruled in favour of granting the company's request.
In your communication you ask me to "take the necessary steps to defer the enforcement of that ruling." In this respect, I wish to call to your attention the provisions of sections 51 and 52 of the Railway Act which grants to the board of transport commissioners, to the governor in council or to the Supreme Court of Canada, as the case may be, the exclusive right to vary or rescind a decision of the board of transport commissioners.
In other words, the board is a court of justice against whose decision an appeal may be lodged, the procedure of which is clearly established by the Railway Act. You will note that the act does not authorize the Minister of Transport to intervene in the way you suggest.
If therefore any of the parties concerned in this investigation wishes to lodge an appeal against the board's decision, it can do so by complying with the above-mentioned provisions of the Railway Act.
As for your commentaries concerning the commercial relationship between the Northern Electric Company and the Bell Telephone Company, I would refer you to the findings of the board of transport commissioners. From page 36 to page 46 of the mimeographed French version, you will find set out in detail the terms of the contract for services between these two companies. You will notice more particularly on page 46 the following statement: "Reading of the agreement, of the documentary evidence and of the minutes of proceedings proves to my satisfaction that the company pays the Northern Electric Co. prices which are not unreasonable."
In view of the fact that I have not sufficient authority to grant your request, I feel I must reject it.
I am sorry not to be able to give you a more favourable reply and I thank you for obliging me with your views in this matter.
The Address-Mr. haCroix To the above letter from the Minister of Transport, I replied as follows on December 11, 1950:
My dear Minister,
I acknowledge your letter of December 4 concerning the decision of the board of transport commissioners approving the revision of some of the Bell Telephone Company's rates in the district of Quebec.
You draw to my attention the provisions of sections 51 and 52 of the Railway Act which grants to the board of transport commissioners, the governor in council or the Supreme Court of Canada, as the case may be, the exclusive right to vary or rescind a decision of the board of transport commissioners. That is exactly what I did when I wrote to you on November 20 since I asked you in your capacity as Minister of Transport to be so good as to appeal to the governor in council of which you are part.
I understand and I have always understood that parliament has the right to appeal to the governor in council; this will probably be done shortly since you will receive petitions from every town concerned as well as from chambers of commerce begging the governor in council to intervene in this matter.
With respect to the business relationship between the Northern Electric Co. and the Bell Telephone Co., you refer me to pages 36 and 46 of the French copy of the board of transport commissioners' judgment, which deals m detail with the contract for services between these two companies. From page 46 you draw the following statement: "Reading of the agreement, of the documentary evidence and of the minutes of proceedings proves to my satisfaction that the company pays the Northern Electric Co. prices which are not unreasonable."
How then could the board of transport commissioners have reached this conclusion if they have not permitted that evidence be based on the aggregate profits made by the Northern Electric which, as you know, belongs to and is controlled by the Bell Telephone?
You know as well as I do that the Bell Telephone Company controls the Northern Electric Co. and that it is paid but a very small dividend on its shares, compared to the profits made. Investigation of the Northern Electric's operations could have easily established the exorbitant figure for depreciation, for salaries paid to officials, under various guises. In addition, you could have discovered that the Bell Telephone Company has erected a building and leased it to the Northern Electric which, in turn, sublets parts of it to the Bell Telephone.
You might also have noticed that all the equipment manufactured by the Northern Electric Company and suitable for construction purposes is entirely turned over to the Bell Telephone Company for use in its new buildings and installations.
I understand that the board of transport commissioners refused to admit any evidence concerning the operations of the Northern Electric Company in general. It seems hardly credible that the conclusion should be reached that the price asked by the Northern Electric Company for its equipment is not unreasonable, since absolutely no account is taken of profits made by this wholly-owned subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company. After all.
106	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. LaCroix these profits should augment the latter company's revenue in all fairness to its shareholders and to the public who pay the rates established on the basis of profits made by the Bell Co. The board of transport commissioners used the expression "not unreasonable prices", in its report, because it was afraid to say "reasonable prices".
Consequently, Mr. Minister, you should not be too surprised if this question is raised once more at the next session of parliament, several members having expressed the opinion that parliament should appeal in this case to the cabinet itself. If you look into the increase in rates, as it particularly affects the Quebec district, you will agree with me that we are right.
I would be very grateful to you if you could intervene in this connection before the governor in council."

I wish to inform the house of these facts so that it may take action and also because I believe they are essential to the campaign now in progress against the exploiting of the mass of the people by those who enjoy special privileges.
One of the best ways to fight communism is to prevent the setting up of trusts and to operate the public or commercial services in the interest of all.

In addition, to promote private enterprise, legislation will be required to break up combines and ensure a better distribution of public wealth.
Before resuming my seat, I wish to mention another matter which, in my opinion, should be called to the government's attention.
In these troubled times, there is someone who can lead us into the path of understanding and avoid a third world war. I refer to the Vatican, the heart of Christendom, where, following the example set by Great Britain and several other countries, we should have an ambassador.
Many diplomats, even those who object to such relationships on purely religious grounds, admit, in private, that in no other place is it possible to obtain so much accurate and detailed information. From every corner of the globe some 2,000 reports reach the Vatican weekly. They are forwarded by some 3,000 archbishops and bishops and 300,000 priests. Such reports, especially those coming from eastern Europe by secret channels, are the best source of information to be found anywhere.
The church uses this source of information to defend itself against communism and to foster the growth of Catholicism the world over. On the basis of such data the Vatican radio is able to furnish its listeners with day and night highly interesting broadcasts in 16 different languages. Russia, Czechoslovakia, Poland and other communist countries favour the Vatican radio with as much attention as the "Voice of America" by jamming the messages sent by the church to its faithful.
A large number of those reports are not published, but diplomats accredited to the Holy See have access to them in certain circumstances.
May I therefore express the hope that, following the lead set by other countries, our leaders will send an ambassador to the Vatican.
I wish to point out too that the people of my constituency were disappointed when they noted that the speech from the throne makes no reference to the adoption of a national flag. At a time when our part in the international sphere takes on added importance from day to day, it is regrettable for our fellow countrymen abroad and for ourselves that we should still be without that symbol around which we

could rally and which would do a great deal to maintain our patriotism and the national unity so necessary to its full expression.
I dare hope that the government will very shortly review its policy in this respect. (Text):

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
First of all I want to join with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) and the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) in expressing my appreciation of the opportunity of having attended the United Nations as parliamentary adviser from one of the opposition groups. I want to endorse what the hon. member for Peel has said regarding the opportunity that was afforded to us as members of the opposition groups to participate with the Canadian delegation in the daily discussions of the program which was to come before the various committees of the United Nations during that session.
I am confident that the practice followed by this government in giving the opposition groups those privileges will help to win support and unity in this house for our policy against any aggressor nations. I should point out, however, that our appreciation is none the less sincere because in our subamendment, moved by the leader of this group, we take issue with government policy regarding the United Nations aggressor resolution.
One of the glories of a democracy as distinguished from totalitarianism is that we have the right and privilege to disagree with the government, or the party in power, according to our conscience and our light. I think that what the hon. member for Peel said regarding the fact that we were free as opposition members to approve or to disapprove of government policy during the discussion periods is exemplified in the fact that some of us who were members of that delegation are now taking issue with the government.
Quite rightly, Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne indicates that our chief concern in this session must be directed to the international crisis with which Canada, along with the rest of the free world, is faced, and with matters that are closely related to that crisis. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) gave us a review of that crisis which faces the free nations of the world, and he laid down certain general principles which, in his opinion, we should follow in meeting that crisis. On the whole I am confident that hon. members, and the country generally, will agree with these general principles which were laid down by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. We all appreciate his awareness of that crisis and his intelligent understanding of it. I might
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy add, we have to await pronouncements from other departments of the government before we can assume that all departments of the government, and the government as a whole, are as fully aware of the crisis as is the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
This evening the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) outlined to us the government's policy of preparedness for meeting that crisis. So far as I was able to follow the minister, I assume that the government policy is as follows. First of all, we are to prepare to defend our own shores in case of an attack. We are to prepare to go to the assistance of our allies of the Atlantic treaty in case they are attacked. We are to prepare to go to the assistance of the United Nations when called upon, to stop aggression anywhere. Finally we are to prepare for the eventuality of a total war. That policy I am confident will have the fullest possible support of every member in the house, and of every political party here represented. Moreover, I am confident it will have the support of every loyal Canadian who wishes to see democracy survive in our country.
The question uppermost in the minds of Canadians today is whether or not we can contain communism without a global atomic war. Canadians do not want to find this country overrun by communists. Canadians do not want to be obliged to live in a communist-controlled world. They do however want to avoid war, if that is possible. It is the hope and prayer of millions of Canadians that communism can be halted without having recourse to such a war. It is the achievement of that objective which is the primary responsibility of governments and diplomats of the free countries of the world. To achieve that objective these governments and diplomats will need the support of the peoples of the countries they represent.
I think we dare not accept the inevitability of war. The mere acceptance of the inevitability of war may very well make war itself inevitable. We are living today in a revolutionary period-probably the greatest revolutionary period in all human history. Tides of revolution are sweeping across the world today. They can no more be stopped than can the tides of the ocean. Nor are those tides of revolution caused necessarily by communism. Without communism, without the threat of Russian imperialism, we would still be faced with these revolutions throughout the world.
The world order as we have known it for the last century is being swept away. A new world order is in process of being born. Whether that new world order is to be communism, or whether we can adjust our democratic society to meet the needs of the

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy peoples of the world, and thereby avert conquest of the world by communists, depends I think upon how speedily democracy can adjust itself, and whether it can adjust itself to meet those needs speedily enough to stop the march of communism.
Eventually we may be forced to have recourse to war-even to atomic war. I cannot for one moment believe that the democratic nations will forgo their freedom and surrender to totalitarianism any more than they were willing to surrender to totalitarian fascism and nazism, without fighting to the bitter end with every weapon at their disposal.
If there is one rallying call that should ring throughout the free world today I would say it should be, "Free peoples of the world, unite! You have nothing to lose but your freedom." Free peoples everywhere will rally to the cause of democracy and, if necessary, fight for it. If the newly freed peoples of Asia, and those who have not yet received their freedom, are to line up on the side of the western nations in the conflict, then democracy as we know it today must do a good deal of housecleaning. In fact, our one hope of saving democracy, either with or without war, lies in the speed with which democracy can bring about those necessary reforms within itself to meet the growing needs of the people of the world today.
Certainly communism is not the answer to those crying needs. Communism is not that good life for which the peoples of the world down through the ages have been seeking. It is not the answer to the revolutionary cries of Asia, Africa and other parts of the east. If communism is not the answer, neither is capitalism. When I refer to capitalism I mean capitalism as it exists on this continent, capitalism as the peoples of Asia have known it for almost two hundred years.
If some of the free nations today which are prepared to spend billions of dollars and millions of lives in defence of democracy would cease to confuse democracy with capitalism as it existed in the past, and be concerned more with democracy per se, in my opinion their task would be easier and their success more assured. Today there are millions of people in Asia and elsewhere who could be induced to fight for democracy. Millions of those people have very little incentive to fight for the type of capitalist democracy they have known over the past centuries.
All parties in the house are agreed that in this crisis the free nations must arm themselves. They must be prepared to fight in defence of their freedom, if that becomes the only alternative. While we all accept that premise, I believe we are agreed that it would


be preferable to avoid war if at all possible, on the theory that communism can be contained without war, and that, given time, democracy may be able to demonstrate its advantages over communism as a way of life, not only to those who live in the non-communist world but to many of those who live in parts of the world now dominated by communism.
That leads us to consider the question of negotiation with Russia. I do not believe for one moment that a general peace agreement, implying agreement on all outstanding problems, is possible with Russia. As far as I know, only one man in history has ever succeeded in making an agreement of that kind with Russia, and that was Hitler. Hitler was able to do so because he shared Russia's taste for dividing the world into spheres of influence. I cannot conceive that the United States or other countries in the United Nations will ever be willing to participate in such a horse-trading deal.
While negotiation for general peace may be impossible, that does not rule out the possibility of negotiation for peace or of agreement within limited areas. It does not rule out the possibility of maintaining an armed peace or armed truce with Russia. The idea of an armed peace is not new in history. Europe lived under an armed peace for forty years between the time of the Franco-Prus-sian war of 1870 and 1914. Granted such a truce is unstable: we know that the armed truce to which I referred eventually led to war in 1914 and any armed truce that we may achieve with Russia may eventually lead to war.
But our best chance of survival is to secure time in which the free countries of the world may not only equip themselves to withstand Russian aggression but be able to adapt themselves to the needs of the people and win support from these millions of Asiatics. Today we are engulfed in a cold war that may last for a generation. Armed peace is not war; it is not necessarily a cold war. It implies a settlement of differences in limited spheres by negotiation, even though the negotiators may parley with atom bombs in their hands. It does not imply commercial or cultural boycotts of nations; it is possible with intense trade and cultural contacts.
I think we are getting on dangerous ground if we accept and become guided by the belief that an atomic war is inevitable, that because communism is our enemy, communism must be blasted from the earth here and now by atomic bombs and the sooner we undertake it the better. That school of thought has a great many supporters in this country and in the United States, in fact far too many supporters. The adoption of that philosophy

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
must lead eventually to a war of annihilation that will set civilization back on its heels for centuries. Those hon. members who received and read copies of the editorial that appeared in Maclean's magazine of January 15 will recall what was said about the possible results of a world war against communism at the present time. Whether we lose such a war, whether we win it or whether it draws to a stalemate, at the conclusion of that war we shall be looking straight down the gun-barrels of world war IV.
War will not wipe communism off the earth; it will no more solve our problems than did world war I or world war II solve the problems of those days. It is on that account that today millions of people are praying that our government and our diplomats may be able to guide us through this period of crisis, may be able to help us withstand the onslaught of communism, may be able to help us to contain communism or to defeat aggression without having recourse to such a world war.
Nevertheless, as I have indicated before, I think as a free people we must be prepared to meet force with force. Above all we must not permit ourselves to be pushed into such a war until we have exhausted every intelligent and honourable means of averting it. Because of the shift in world power which resulted from world war II there has been created a great power vacuum in Europe. Today we find Russia and the United States, two great world powers, vying with each other to occupy that vacuum. Capitalist America and communist Russia are fast dividing the world into two camps and each is seeking allies wherever it can.
The most potential allies that either side can find will be the Asiatic countries. Possibly not from the standpoint of military power, but in the long conflict between communism and democracy, whichever side the 800 million people in Asia choose to throw their weight toward, that side will eventually win. In the struggle for the alliance of Asiatic countries Russia has a great advantage over the western world. For two hundred years these countries have experienced life under western rule. The history of western nations in Asia does very little to win them friends there at this particular time. On the contrary, Russia was not a colonizing country during the
nineteenth century. So far as colonies in Asia and Africa are concerned, Russia has no past. She finds it much easier to appeal to the imagination and the needs of the Asiatic people than do the western countries today. As a matter of fact I think we car. agree that today the sins of capitalism in Asia are coming home to roost. Today we are paying for the sins of the past.
Faced with a revolutionary Asia, we have Russia, a great imperialist power, always on the alert, always ready to avail herself of any opportunity to foment trouble, to make the road of the democratic countries difficult and to undermine their influence. As the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) said this afternoon, they are always on the alert to put the nations of the free world in the international doghouse. That, taken together with the fact that Russia has not the past that the western nations have in Asia, enables us to realize the colossal task facing the western world today if it is to win the support and allegiance of those countries.
I mentioned the fact that democracy must do some housecleaning. We have in Canada a very great degree of political democracy. It has been won for us throughout the centuries by our forebears. We appreciate the freedom of our democratic institutions. We have achieved a considerable degree of economic democracy. The sphere of economic democracy has been widening and increasing with the years. We have in this country and on this continent a considerable degree of industrial democracy. Trade unions are able to participate through collective bargaining in the planning and determining of the policies which industry shall follow. Most of the countries of Asia have very little knowledge of political, economic or industrial democracy. In addition to political, economic and industrial democracy we need to take ethnic democracy to them. The day when the white race can consider itself master of the universe, master of the world, is past. If democracy can reform itself, if we can be given time, we may well be able to avoid global warfare, and we may be able to retain and improve democracy in this country and in other countries of the world.
On motion of Mr. Noseworthy the debate was adjourned.
